modules.title: Servicelink Gateway Training
modules.description: This module provides a comprehensive overview of safety and discrimination, harassment and bullying in the workplace as well as an overview of Servicelink. The topics covered are:

topics.title: Work Health Safety (WHS) Responsibilities
topics.body: Employers WHS law places a duty of care on the employer to provide a healthy and safe working environment. The employer must ensure they do whatever they can (in other words, whatever is ‘reasonably practicable’) to ensure that workers and other persons are not put at risk from work carried out as part of their business. Moreover, the employer must ensure that the following are without risks to health and safety: the workplace, including entry and exit and anything arising from the workplace; the fixtures, fittings or plant; the plant, substance or structure. You should receive necessary instruction, supervision and training from both your employer and anybody else responsible for the management and control of your workplace. Not only will you complete this induction, but you should also receive a workplace and company specific induction from your employer prior to commencing work. You should also receive job specific training, instruction and supervision as necessary from a suitably qualified individual. Workers As a ‘worker’, you have a duty of care; this duty is to take reasonable care for your own health and safety, as well as others. You must also co-operate with the employer in compliance with the WHS legislation, this includes following any policy or procedure that has been notified to workers and implemented by the employer to ensure health and safety at the workplace.

topics.title: Risk Management
topics.body:
Having an effective risk management process in the workplace is critical to ensure that work activities are not likely to harm anyone. There needs to be awareness of what could possibly go wrong (the likelihood of an incident occurring), and the potential consequences (what harm could be caused if there is an incident). The four key risk management steps that you need to be aware of, and ensure the Employer has in place are: identify hazards – find out what could cause harm; assess risk – understand the likelihood of a hazard causing harm and how serious it could be; control risks – implement the most effective control measures that is reasonably practicable in the circumstances; and review control measures to ensure they are working as planned.

Consultation

If we don’t report hazards, they may not be acted on, and if we don´t give our suggestions to what controls might work well, the hazard may not be adequately managed; therefore, consultation is a very important process to the risk management process. It is also a duty of the employer to consult on matters that can directly affect your health and safety. So what is Consultation? Consultation is a 3 step process, it involves: sharing of information; giving workers a reasonable opportunity to express views; and taking those views into account before making decisions on health and safety matters. As a worker your employer owes you a duty to consult with you, ensuring that you have an opportunity to express your views on matters that may directly affect your health and safety.

topics.title: Issue Resolution
topics.body: So what’s the process if you need to raise a health and safety issue? The employer that you are working for may have an agreed issue resolution procedure, therefore you would need to make yourself aware of this procedure and follow the process. Generally, an issue resolution procedure requires the following steps: Report the health and safety issue to your Manager and the health and safety representative (HSR) (if there is one), Discuss the issue with your Manager and HSR, If the discussions do not lead to a resolution, any party can contact the relevant State Health & Safety Authority who will send an inspector to the workplace to assist in resolving the health and safety issue. This request should only be made after reasonable efforts have been made to achieve an effective resolution of the issue.

topics.title: Your Responsibility
topics.body:
What are you responsible for as an employee? Take reasonable care to protect your own health and safety, and others potentially affected by your actions at work. Comply with all laws, policies, procedures and safety instructions. Co-operate with your employer on any actions taken to ensure health and safety. This includes: Following workplace health and safety policies and procedures; Using risk control measures provided to you; Attending workplace health and safety training; Reporting hazards and risks in the workplace. Hold licences, permits or qualifications as required. Equipment, including personal protective equipment must be used by you as directed, stored appropriately and kept in good working condition. Report all workplace hazards, mishaps, and incidents, including near misses on the day they occur. Incidents should be reported to your employer and your workplace manager or Supervisor.

Starting your new role

When starting in your new role you should receive a company induction which introduces you to the workplace and the workplace policies and procedures. Following your company induction, you should receive appropriate information, instruction, training and supervision to ensure that you can do your work safely and minimise the risk to your health. Your training should: Show you how to carry out your job safely; Include a competency assessment through demonstration before starting the work or starting each new task; A demonstration on how to use the necessary equipment and how to safely wear/use any protective gear, such as gloves, safety footwear and goggles; Explanation of health and safety policies and procedures; Workplace tour and understanding of the workplace layout; Introduction to your immediate supervisor, health and safety representative and workmates. At the start of your job your Supervisor should ensure that you are closely and competently supervised. Responsible, mature and necessary supervision must be provided by your Supervisor on an ongoing basis. It is critical that you understand your right to raise safety, discrimination, or harassment issues with your employer and to do so without fear of victimisation. You are also entitled and encouraged to have someone represent you on workplace health and safety matters – a health and safety representative (HSR). If your workplace does not have an HSR, you or any other employee can request to set up a designated work group (DWG) structure. Once a DWG is established an HSR needs to be elected. If you are injured or involved in a ‘near miss’ safety incident you should immediately notify your employer. A near miss is an unplanned event that does not cause injury, damage or ill health but could do so and reporting them is a really important way of staying on top of safety. Reporting helps everyone to identify hazards and inappropriate conduct, prevent their occurrence and ensure your safety and equality.

topics.title: Common Workplace Hazards
topics.body:
Whilst there are a number of people who are responsible for workplace safety you play a key role in identifying hazards and unsafe work practices. Some of the most common hazards in the workplace are: Work practices involving constant bending, lifting and twisting of your body Objects and liquids left on floors which result in slips, trips and falls Moving machinery parts which could crush or cut body parts Vehicles such as forklifts and trucks which may collide with workers Non-existent or confusing evacuation procedures Exposure to chemicals and other hazardous substances Bullying and harassment that results in psychological illness or physical assault Poor ergonomic design and practices that result in muscular strain

Identifying Risks and Safety Issues

Before commencing work, you should ensure that you know who to report safety issues to. Most workplaces will have procedures for handling issues when they arise; they’re often called issue resolution procedures. If there is no such procedure in your workplace you should notify your employer or Supervisor and they should follow it up for you. When issues are raised one or more of the following things should occur: 1. The issue raised will be assessed to determine the level of risk. 2. Individuals in the workplace who are responsible for health and safety will decide on the best solution. 3. A timeframe will be agreed for correcting the problem. 4. The effectiveness of the solution will be monitored.

Responsibilities in the Workplace

The Health and Safety Act and Regulations place duties on Officers, Person’s Conducting a Business or Undertaking (PCBUs)/Employers/Hosts and workers to manage the risk of musculoskeletal disorder associated with hazardous manual handling tasks. Each party is responsible for workplace safety, including manual tasks. In summary:

topics.title: Safe Lifting Techniques
topics.body:
It’s important to use safe lifting technique, which includes: Planning the lift Positioning yourself over the load Bending your knees to get in the correct position to lift with your legs, not your back Taking a secure grip Keeping the load in close to the body, and Lifting smoothly whilst keeping your back straight and your head looking forward.

Use & Storage of PPE

To ensure that your PPE provides the level of protection that is it designed to, PPE should: Be appropriate for the type of work and give appropriate protection for the risk Give you adequate protection from the hazard that you may be exposed to Not create additional health or safety risks Be compatible with other PPE being used (e.g ear muffs with a hard hat) Fit properly Not interfere with any medical conditions of the user Be easy to use Be comfortable Comply with relevant Australian Standards When your employer provides you with your PPE they should: Instruct and train you in the use of the PPE; Ensure that it fits correctly; Display appropriate signs to remind you and your workmates when you need to wear your PPE. PPE should be stored in a clean environment and needs to be checked regularly to identify any damage or defects that need to be repaired or discarded. If you identify any damage or defects to your PPE ensure that you report this immediately to your Supervisor.

topics.title: Ergonomics
topics.body:
Ergonomics is the scientific study of human performance at work. It considers human abilities and limitations when designing or arranging workplaces, products and systems so that they can best fit the people who use them. This process aims to reduce the risk of occupational overuse syndrome. Occupational overuse relates to how you do your job. Occupational overuse used to be called RSI which was short for repetitive strain injury. It occurs where there is repetitive movement or sustained unnatural or forceful movement during the performance of your job. OOS includes a range of injuries and conditions that include symptoms of discomfort or persistent pain in muscles, tendons and other soft tissues. Poorly designed equipment or workstations, repetitive movements and awkward work postures and movements contribute to the OOS injuries and conditions.

How to Correct Poor Ergonomics

Your employer has a responsibility to identify any work processes or equipment that could lead to OOS. Additionally, they need to implement controls to eliminate or reduce the risk of sustaining such injuries or conditions. Controls can include: Providing appropriate equipment and workstations for the job, such as ergonomically designed, adjustable furniture, chairs, desks and computers. Ensuring that the work area is arranged so that the materials, equipment and controls can be easily reached without stretching or twisting. Ensuring that hand tools for repetitive tasks are a comfortable size, shape and weight, are well-balanced with a comfortable grip, and require no more than reasonable force to operate. Providing training and information to employees about safe working practices, for example correct work methods and postures and the correct use of tools, machinery and other equipment. Ensuring that equipment is regularly maintained and replaced as needed, and that new equipment is assessed on health and safety grounds before purchase.

Improving your ergonomics

How can you improve your ergonomics? Ensure the backrest and height of your chair are adjusted to fit the curve of your back and allow a slightly reclined posture; Ensure the seat height and the angle are adjusted so that you can sit with your feet flat on the floor and hips between 90 degrees & 120 degrees; Use an adjustable height footrest if, after you have adjusted the height of your chair, your feet do not sit flat on the floor; Adjust the desk height so that the surface is just below your elbow height; If the desk is not adjustable, is the surface set just below your elbow height?; Place frequently used items on the desk in an easy to reach position; Store large and heavy items within close reach and not above shoulder height; Organise your work to mix repetitive with non-repetitive tasks; Introduce frequent short breaks if your job can not be varied or rotated; It is important that you report any symptoms of OOS early to identify and treat the condition whilst it can be managed. If you experience any physical discomfort as a result of performing your work tasks, report it immediately to your Supervisor.

What to do if you are injured

Unfortunately, injuries occur in even the safest of workplaces. It is essential that you understand what to do if you are injured at the workplace: Notify your Supervisor or First Aid Officer regardless of how minor the injury may appear at first. Keep your employer (HR) informed of your condition and progress at all times as they have a responsibility to report the incident. If you cannot attend work because of the injury or you incur related medical costs, hold discussions with your employer about the completion and lodgement of a worker’s compensation claim form. This should be done as soon as possible after the injury occurs.

Stress

Did you know workplace stress is the second most common cause of workplace compensation claims in Australia after manual handling? Stress claims cost businesses $10.11 billion p.a. due to loss of productivity and absenteeism. This figure is likely to be under-represented however as it doesn’t include unsuccessful claims and those who do not make a formal claim. So what does stress actually mean? The World Health Organisation defines stress as “the reaction people may have when presented with demands and pressures that are not matched to their knowledge and abilities and which challenge their ability to cope”. Stress can occur in a wide range of situations, is complex and typically has multiple causes. Many jobs involve negative factors that put unwanted pressure (stress) on the worker, leading to adverse consequences. Stress is not a disease or injury in itself, but can lead to mental and physical ill health, and can also be a factor in workplace incidents.

topics.title: What Causes Workplace Stress
topics.body:
Negative Stress

So, how is negative stress identified in the workplace? There are many different potential work-related stress hazards and risks in the workplace. You should be aware of systematic processes that the organisation undertakes to identify these hazards and risks. These processes should involve consultation with the workforce including you as a worker. Risks to psychological health in the workplace can largely be categorised as those relating to the social and physical work environment, the way that work is organised (system of work) and the way that work is managed. Some aspects of the social and physical environment that have the potential to cause harm are: role in the organisation career development, status and pay conflicting home/work demands physical work environment and equipment

Stress and Systems of Work

Issues relating to the way that work is organised (system of work) can include: the content and demands of the work the workload and pace of the work work schedules and working hours the extent of participation and control that people have over the work The way that work is managed can have harmful effects relating to: inadequate or unsupportive supervision lack of suitable information, instruction and training to enable employees to do their work

Identifying & Managing Stress

As a worker your employer owes you a duty of care. This duty of care extends to ensuring that your health and safety is not at risk; the meaning of health includes ‘psychological health’. Duty holders should be taking reasonable steps to eliminate or reduce the risk of negative stress. If you are a contractor, the on-hire/contracting firm can play a significant role in identifying and managing negative stress. Expect that your on-hire/contracting firm does the following: provides you with key job information (tasks, safety aspects, working hours including overtime, expected break times, remote work or working in isolation, reporting structure) maintains regular contact with you and offers opportunities to report any health and safety concerns associated with the contract assignment. For the Host, expect systems to manage the following areas: work environment systems of work work tasks If you feel you are exposed to negative stressors – report it to your supervisor/manager and (if appropriate) you’re on hire/contracting firm!

topics.title: Sexual Harassment
topics.body: Sexual harassment is any unwelcome behaviour of a sexual nature that can make a person feel humiliated, intimidated or offended. Sexual harassment may include but is not be limited to: Sexual harassment can be intentional or unintentional and is not sexual interaction, flirtation, attraction or friendship which is invited, mutual, or consensual.

topics.title: Sexual Harassment and the Law
topics.body: A single incident may amount to sexual harassment depending on the circumstances. For example, a single remark may be so offensive as to amount to sexual harassment in itself, but an unwanted invitation out may not constitute sexual harassment if it is not repeated. Sexual harassment is unlawful in any work-related context, including conferences, work functions, office parties and business or field trips and includes interactions with clients and customers. Sexual harassment is prohibited under Australian State and Federal legislation as well as international legislation.

topics.title: Workplace Harassment
topics.body:
As in sexual harassment, it can be seen as 'workplace harassment' if you are subjected to repeated behaviour, by a person, including your employer or a colleague or group of colleagues and:

Workplace harassment can be intentional or unintentional. Examples of the more common types of behaviours that may be regarded as workplace harassment (if the behaviour is repeated or occurs as part of a pattern of behaviour) include: abusing a person loudly, either in private or when others are present; repeated threats of dismissal or other severe punishment for no reason; constant ridicule and being put down; leaving offensive messages on email, telephone or potentially via social media; sabotaging a person's work, for example, deliberately withholding or supplying incorrect information, hiding documents or equipment, and not passing on messages; maliciously excluding and isolating a person from workplace activities; persistent and unjustified criticisms, often about petty, irrelevant or insignificant matters; humiliating a person through gestures, sarcasm, criticism and insults, both in private or in front of customers, Managers or other staff; and spreading gossip or false, malicious rumours about a person with or without an intent to cause the person harm.

Victimisation

It’s also against the law to threaten or treat people less favourably as a result of them raising or supporting allegations of discrimination, harassment or bullying. It may be considered victimisation if a person has suffered some form of detriment because they have, for example, lodged a complaint of discrimination or sexual harassment, attended a conciliation conference or reasonably asserted their rights, or supported someone else’s rights.

topics.title: Bullying
topics.body:
Examples of behaviour, whether intentional or unintentional, that may be considered workplace bullying is if it is repeated, unreasonable and creates a risk to health and safety. This includes but is not limited to:

Your Duty

The health and safety of a co-worker doesn’t only relate to their physical wellbeing, it also includes their emotional or mental health. Treating someone in an undermining or unreasonable way negatively impacts upon their health and safety. You also have a duty to comply with any reasonable instruction provided to you and co-operate with any reasonable policies and procedures, such as a workplace bullying policy.

topics.title: What is not Bullying?
topics.body:
Sometimes in the work environment decisions are made that you won’t like, or don’t agree with. There are also some situations where people in the workplace will have disagreements or differences of opinion and these are not generally considered to be workplace bullying. People can have differences and disagreements in the workplace without engaging in repeated, unreasonable behaviour that creates a risk to health and safety. The key point here is that just because you don’t agree with a decision or an opinion doesn’t mean that it amounts to bullying.

modules.title: On-Hired Employee Safety
modules.description: This module provides an introduction to “on-hired employment”, sometimes known as ‘temping’, ‘contracting’ and ‘labour hire’. The module provides a general overview of: This module will take about 30 minutes to complete, not including the assessment

topics.title: Learning Outcomes
topics.body: You’re about to complete the on-hired worker safety induction module. Keep in mind that in addition to this module, you may also be required to complete additional induction/training modules relevant to a job you may be assigned to. When you have completed this induction, you should know the following: Who is responsible for safety in on-hire work What unsafe work is What to do if you encounter unsafe work in on-hired assignment What to do if you are injured at work

topics.title: WHS
topics.body: WHS is short for Work Health and Safety and is now commonly referred to as work safety. WHS involves, amongst other things: Employers, and other persons running businesses and the like, ensuring that they are providing and maintaining a workplace that is safe and without risk to health; and Workers caring for themselves and other people in the workplace as well as observing and respecting all safety rules, directions and requirements relating to health and safety Remember safe workplaces require involvement from everyone, not just employers and business operators.

topics.title: On-Hire Work
topics.body: Knowing who is responsible for your safety in on-hire work is especially important because of the increased number of people and organisations involved and the potential for increased confusion and uncertainty. The form of work you are preparing for, or may have already started, is one whereby the organisation that employs (or you if you are a contractor) ‘on-hires’ you to work for one of their clients under the client’s general guidance and instruction. You may also know of this way of working as: Temping Contract work Agency work Labour Hire For consistency and simplicity, we will collectively refer to this way of working as ‘on-hire work’ during this induction module, and you will be known as an ‘on-hire worker’.

topics.title: Employers, Principals and Host Organisations
topics.body: What you may call the Employment Agency, or contracting firm, is actually your employer, if you are employed to work as an on-hire worker. If you are engaged as an independent contractor the contracting firm is called the Principal or Hirer. To simplify things, regardless of whether you are an employee or an independent contractor, we will call the organisation that is engaging you, the employer. Your employer and others are responsible for your safety in on-hire work. Your employer’s client, where you are assigned to work and receive your day to day instructions, is called the host organisation. The host organisation has the same obligation as your employer to ensure your safety. But because you are not under the immediate and direct control of your legal employer or hirer, your co-operation is more important than ever. There is also an obligation upon the organisation, and their workers, working within a host organisation’s workplace, to co-operate and co-ordinate with one another to ensure the safety of workers.

topics.title: Responsibilities
topics.body: As was just mentioned, your employer, or hirer, and the host organisation are responsible for your health and safety. You should receive instruction, supervision and training from both your employer and the host organisation, or the host organisations representative. Following the completion of this safety induction you should also complete a site/company specific induction with your host organisation prior to commencing work at their workplace as well as job specific training and instruction. If you don’t receive these additional inductions and training let your employer or hirer know.

topics.title: Changing Duties & Raising Issues
topics.body: Only perform work in accordance with the job or assignment description provided by your employer. If the host organisation directs you to do work that differs from the original description then you should first obtain authorisation from your employer. You have a right to raise safety issues with both your employer and the host organisation, but be polite and try and provide a solution, not just a problem, where possible. If you feel you are being treated poorly by your host organisation, or any other organisation working within a host organisation’s workplace because you raise a genuine safety issue or concern, notify your employer or hirer immediately – their behaviour is illegal. If you are injured or involved in a near miss you must notify both your employer or hirer and the host organisation.

topics.title: Your Employer’s Responsibility
topics.body: Your employer, or hirer, is responsible for ensuring you are placed in a job that is safe and without risk to your health. This includes a responsibility to co-operate with other organisations which may control or influence the way you work whilst on assignment. You must have the skills and experience to perform the job safely as well as receive information, instruction and training on the job to be performed. This instruction and training should be provided by both your employer, or hirer, and the host organisation. Your employer, or hirer, is required to work in partnership with the host organisation to assess risks and to ensure the maintenance of safe systems of work, machinery, equipment and the safe use of materials. Your employer, or hirer, and the host organisation are also obliged to supply any specialised personal protective equipment (PPE) that you may require.

topics.title: The Host Organisation’s Responsibility
topics.body: By law, a host organisation has virtually the same responsibilities as your employer, or hirer, to provide a safe workplace, to maintain safe systems of work, to ensure the safe use of materials and provide any specialised personal protective equipment (PPE). The host organisation must also provide you with information, training and supervision to enable you to work safely. A host organisation must not change your job without obtaining approval from your employer. Any change to your job must be discussed, and assessed as being safe before you commence work, so that you are capable of working safely.

topics.title: Your Responsibility
topics.body: You must take reasonable care to protect your own health and safety, and others potentially affected by your actions at work. You must comply with all work safety laws, policies, procedures and safety instructions. This includes instructions from the host organisation and other organisations who are responsible for the way you work on assignments. Equipment, including personal protective equipment (PPE) must be used by you as directed and kept in good working condition. You must immediately report all hazards, incidents and injuries to both your employer or hirer and the host organisation.

topics.title: Responding to Safety Issues
topics.body: There are a number of people responsible for the management of health and safety issues at the host organisation’s workplace including: Your supervisor WHS Representatives, where they exist Members of your employer’s, or the host organisations, WHS committee Your employer Your host organisation You Before commencing your assignment at the host organisation’s workplace, you should ensure that you know who to report safety issues to. If you’re not told, ask!

topics.title: Issue Resolution Procedures
topics.body:
Most workplaces will have procedures for handling work safety issues when they arise, they’re often called issue resolution procedures. If there is no such procedure in place at the host organisations workplace you should contact your employer or hirer and they can follow it up for you. If you’re unsure about something relating to safety in the workplace, and you don’t want to upset your host organisation, contact your employer and get them to contact the host organisation. You have a right to be heard without fear of being treated differently

Responding to WHS Issues

When issues are raised one or more of the following things should occur: 1. The issue should be assessed to determine the level of risk. 2. Individuals in the workplace who are responsible for health and safety should decide what the best solution is. 3. A timeframe should be agreed for correcting the problem. 4. The effectiveness of the solution should be monitored

topics.title: Unsafe Work
topics.body: Whilst there are a number of people who are responsible for workplace safety you play a key role in identifying hazards and unsafe work practices. A hazard is something that has the potential to cause harm to people or property. Workplace hazards can be present in many forms and the effects of hazards aren’t always immediate, they can develop over time.

topics.title: Hazards at Work
topics.body: Some of the most common hazards in the workplace are: Work practices involving constant bending, lifting and twisting of your body Objects and liquids left on floors which result in slips, trips and falls Moving machinery parts which could crush or cut body parts Vehicles such as forklifts and trucks which may collide with workers Non-existent or confusing evacuation procedures Exposure to chemicals and other hazardous substances Harassment that results in psychological illness or physical assault Poor ergonomic design and practices that result in muscular strain Because on-hire workers are not always familiar with the host organisation workplace, it is important that you feel confident to perform the work before commencing. Don’t be rushed by others just because they have been there for longer or because they work directly for the host organisation.

topics.title: Identifying and Reporting Hazards & Risks
topics.body: We’ve just outlined what a hazard is. It’s also very important that you understand that all employees, including on-hired workers, play a critical role in identifying and reporting potential incidents and near misses in the workplace. Incidents also include damage to property. So what should you do as an on-hired worker when you identify a hazard or witness an incident in relation to your job or the job of someone working in the same workplace?

topics.title: What to do when you Identify a Hazard
topics.body: The immediate action you should take upon identifying a hazard is: If you have not been given specific instructions on how to deal with any immediate hazards or incidents you should ask the closest worker to isolate others from any immediate hazard whilst you notify your supervisor. You should follow the instructions of your supervisor or other appropriate persons unless this will expose you to risk. When it is safe to do so, and you are no longer required to assist in the process or risk management you should notify your employer. Remember, your employer is the employment agency. This should be done at a time when it does not impact on the continuation of safe work.

topics.title: What to do if you are Injured
topics.body: Unfortunately injuries occur even in the safest workplaces. It is essential that you understand what to do if you are injured at work. Seek medical attention if you are directed by your Supervisor or the First Aid Officer. Notify your supervisor or First Aid Officer regardless of how minor the injury may appear at first. Notify your employer or hirer as soon reasonably practicable, even if you have already notified the host organisation. Keep your employer or hirer informed of your condition and progress at all times as your employer and the host organisation have specific responsibilities to report on the incident. If you cannot attend work because of the injury or you incur related medical costs, then hold discussions with your employer about the completion and lodgement of a workers compensation claim form. This should be done as soon as possible after the injury occurs. Receiving workers compensations claims is your employer or hirer’s responsibility, not the host organisation.

topics.title: Summary
topics.body: Remember the following essentials about on-hire work and work safety: The agency, or contracting firm, is your employer or principal and is jointly responsible for work safety Your host organisation is also responsible for your safety at work Don’t do work that you have not been trained to do or is not being adequately supervised Always notify your employer or principal if your host organisation changes your duties and don’t do what you think may be unsafe work until the risks are assessed and controlled Report risks, issues and injuries to your employer or hirer, especially if you don’t feel comfortable notifying your host organisation You are now required to complete an assessment to ensure you understood what has just been included in this induction. Good luck!

topics.title: Completion of Learning Section
topics.body: You have completed the learning section of the On-Hired Employment Safety Induction Module. To finalise the training, it is necessary to undertake a short assessment to ensure you have a good understanding of the module content. modules.title: Office Worker Safety
modules.description: This module provides an overview of Office Safety Procedures, including: This module will take about 30 minutes to complete, not including the assessment

topics.title: Introduction
topics.body:
You’re about to complete the office worker safety induction module. It’s general safety induction training for individuals working in an office environment. Before we get started, just remember that this induction is only one part of preparing you to work safely. This course deals with general job safety and should be followed up with a site specific induction as well as specific work activity training that is delivered by your employer, principal, project manager or host organisation before you start working. You should allow about 30 minutes to complete and includes a competency-based assessment.

Learning Outcomes

Once you’ve completed this induction you should have a better understanding of the following: The most common hazards and risks in an office environment; What you can do to prevent these risks injuring someone or making them ill, and Broader safe work principles that should be applied on a day to day basis.

topics.title: Typical Hazards and Risks
topics.body: Whilst offices may appear to be safe and low risk, there are many hazards in and around the office that can result in injury. Some of the most persistent injuries have in fact arisen in office environments, either as a result of the environment or because of the type of work being done. The good news is that in most cases these hazards are very simple to prevent. So, let’s take a closer look. A hazard is anything that has the potential to cause injury or illness to you or damage to property around you and a risk is the likelihood of injury or illness arising from exposures to these hazards. The most common hazards and risks in an office environment arise because of the following: Poor housekeeping, including electrical equipment, and slips, trips and falls Stress Poor ergonomics as a result of setting up your workstation incorrectly Long working hours without regular rest breaks Incorrect bending, lifting and twisting, otherwise known as hazardous manual tasks Poor or non-existent emergency response procedures There certainly are others, but these are some of the most common risks contributing to injury within the office.

topics.title: House Keeping
topics.body: Let’s kick off with housekeeping. You’d be amazed at how many injuries are caused by things that are really easy to fix. Housekeeping’s one of them. Some of the fundamentals of office housekeeping are as follows: Maintain a clean and tidy work area; Don’t run leads across hallways and pedestrian traffic areas; Walk cautiously and slowly when approaching blind corners, especially when carrying objects; Make sure emergency exits are not blocked by storage items or by waste and rubbish; Place paper and cardboard waste into the suitable bin for recycling; Ensure power boards are not overloaded; Don’t overload shelves or cupboards; Don’t place heaters too close to walls or in confined areas where they might overheat; and Turn off electrical appliances at the end of the day. The key here is to take responsibility - don’t think somebody else is going to take care of it. Whilst general housekeeping is a great start, there are, of course, more specific items and practices that can result in hazards and risks, including: Equipment Electrical devices or attachments Slips, trips and falls Hazardous chemicals, Storage; and Manual tasks and occupational overuse Workstation

topics.title: Equipment
topics.body: Equipment includes everything from cutting implements to photocopiers, fax machines, office furniture and workstation equipment. Equipment which is used in the wrong way or poorly maintained can lead to accidental injury. So, make sure you get proper instruction on how to use equipment and don’t presume all equipment is the same. In the best office environments there should be safe operating procedures available to assist with training and safe use. Don’t be afraid to ask for them, and if there are no procedures available, consult the instruction booklet that came with the equipment.

topics.title: Electrical Safety
topics.body: I’m sure I don’t need to tell you that electricity can kill and non-fatal accidents can cause permanent injury. Poor electrical installations may also lead to fires. So make sure you switch off and disconnect electrical appliances that seem faulty, and report it so that it can be repaired or replaced. Another thing, make sure you keep electrical devices and attachments well away from water. Water is typically found in kitchens, bathrooms and drinking cups in offices, so don’t go putting power boards, double adaptors or other devices in kitchens and bathrooms, and watch where you leave glasses and mugs. Electrical extension cords on the floor can be a trip hazard. They are also easily damaged by trolleys and chair castors, which can present an electrical hazard. Other electrical hazards in the office can result from overloading power boards and using unauthorised or modified plugs. These can lead to electrocution or fire. Damaged and frayed power cords also increase the risk of these hazards.

topics.title: Identifying faulty electrical equipment
topics.body: If you notice the following you should take the simple step to report the matter using the hazard reporting process at your workplace: extension socket is cracked and split; a lead has had heavy objects dropped on it, causing broken and deformed insulation; a plug top shows signs of heat damage - further use could cause a fire. Where many power boards are used, report this to your Manager, as a qualified electrician may be required to provide additional outlets. Qualified persons may also be engaged by your employer to test and tag electrical equipment at appropriate intervals.

topics.title: Slips, Trips & Falls
topics.body: Slips, trips and fall hazards are a major source of office incidents and injuries. Slippery floor surfaces are a hazard and often cause a slip when someone walks on it. This can be avoided easily by the prompt clean-up of spilled materials. Inappropriate footwear is also a contributing factor to incidents involving a slip. Obstructions and uneven surfaces are primary trip hazards and these can be avoided by ensuring that floor surfaces are clear and even. So, how do we fall in the office? ... This is usually a result of standing on chairs or shelves to reach upper storage levels. Falls can also occur on poorly designed or badly lit stairwells or worn stair edges. Slips, trips and falls result in thousands of injuries every year. Most common are musculoskeletal injuries, as well as cuts, bruises, fractures and dislocations. Some of the ways you can manage the risk of slips, trips & falls include: Prompt cleaning of spilled materials; Use of ‘slippery when wet’ signage; Appropriate footwear; Reporting slip, trip and fall hazards; Using handrails when accessing stairs;

topics.title: Hazardous Chemicals and the MSDS/SDS
topics.body: Read warning labels on containers and follow manufacturer’s instructions in relation to storage. If you come into contact with or breathe in a hazardous chemical, get a copy of the material safety data sheet (MSDS)/safety data sheet (SDS), which will tell you how to handle the exposure. A MSDS/SDS is a guide provided by manufacturers that outlines everything from how dangerous something is through to what to do if you are exposed to the substance. They should be available near all chemicals and substances that are stored in the office.

topics.title: Manual Tasks
topics.body: I now want to take a look at how you can ensure good manual handling practices in the office. Manual tasks are those tasks that involve bending, lifting and twisting and may include moving boxes or storage items, filing, moving equipment, pushing or pulling trolleys, and filling the printer or photocopier with paper. Remember to use suitable mechanical aids when possible, including trolleys and raised platforms. Suitable storage of materials in the office will minimise the risk of accidents occurring. When filing or storing, the most commonly used items should be placed according to bulk and weight in readily accessible areas between knee and shoulder height. Don’t put heavy items up high because it will put extra strain on you when you try to get them down again, not to mention the likelihood of them dropping on top of you. Check in with your Manager if you are concerned about performing manual tasks. Safe lifting techniques are an administrative control; therefore, they should be considered as the last control to managing the risk. Discuss with your Manager alternative controls for manual tasks before adopting the safe lifting technique

topics.title: Safe Lifting
topics.body: Perform safe lifting techniques, as follows: Plan the lift Position yourself over the load Bend your knees to get in the correct position to lift with your legs, not your back Take a secure grip Pull and keep the load in close to the body, and Lift it smoothly whilst keeping your back straight and your head looking forward.

topics.title: Occupational Overuse
topics.body: Occupational overuse relates to how you do your job. Occupational overuse used to be called RSI which was short for repetitive strain injury. It occurs where there is repetitive movement or sustained unnatural or forceful movement during the performance of your job. It’s essential that you don’t do repetitive work for too long without a break. Make sure you organise and vary your tasks. Occupational overuse is a good example of how injuries can occur in the office from what would otherwise appear to be simple work. I remember an office worker getting occupational overuse syndrome from simply stamping documents without taking a break. So, work with your supervisor to make sure you get variety in your role.

topics.title: Task Variety & Rest Breaks
topics.body: To reduce the risk of sustaining a musculoskeletal disease (MSD) from occupational overuse, it is important to include task variety in the design of work and to take regular rest breaks. Varying your tasks throughout the day provides you with a change in posture and muscles used to perform the work. Sometimes there is not the option for you to alternate keyboarding and computer tasks with other tasks and in this case it’s important to take regular rest or work breaks. Frequent short pauses are preferable to infrequent longer pauses. Breaks can range from the defined breaks such as tea and lunch breaks to short walks to the printer and around the office. In addition to the task variety and rest breaks, the use of office exercises can be useful. Exercises should not be used as a sole control to preventing MSD but can be used in combination with other controls recommended in this module. Exercises should be gentle stretches which provide rest for frequently used muscles and movement for muscles which have been static. The best exercise is usually to get up from a seated position and move around.

topics.title: Work Stations
topics.body: I now want to turn our attention to something that we spend most of our time interacting with in the office - our work station. A work station can be made up of a range of things but generally includes a desk, chair, computer, telephone, drawers, keyboard and mouse. Given the amount of time most office workers spend at their work station it’s vital for it to be set up correctly. Injury can sneak up over a long period of time when you have an incorrectly set up workstation or we don’t interact with it properly. I’m going to run through each part of the work station one by one and outline correct set up and procedure. If you’re sitting at a work station whilst completing this safety induction you might want to think about how you could be better set up right now. But before we start I want you to remember a general safety principle - it’s not good to spend too long sitting at your work station. Try getting up every 20 - 30 minutes, even if it’s to go to the printer or just stretch. Good for the mind as well! Also, remember that it’s important to get your chair set up correctly and then adjust your desk to your chair and seating posture rather than the other way ‘round.

topics.title: Chair Height & Backrest
topics.body: Firstly, adjust your chair height so your feet are comfortably flat on the floor, your thighs are horizontal and your lower legs vertical. Just think of a ninety-degree angle at your knees. If your seat is tilt adjustable, set it to horizontal initially, although you may wish to adjust the tilt slightly forward to suit your comfort. Now that you’ve got the height of your chair seat sorted, let’s look at the backrest for those of you that have one that’s adjustable. Start by raising the backrest to its maximum height. Then sit in the chair and check the fit of the back rest to the curve of the lower back. If not comfortable, lower the height accordingly. Adjust the position of the back rest forward or back until a comfortable pressure is exerted on the lower back area while seated in the usual working posture at the desk. The back-rest position should not feel as though it pushes you out of the seat or that you have to lean too far back to reach it. There should be a two-finger clearance between the front of the chair and the back of the knee.

topics.title: Under Desks & Storage on Top of Desks
topics.body: It’s important not to clutter underneath your desk because this will limit your ability to work naturally and avoid adopting a twisted or awkward posture of the spine. General items, such as computer hard disk drives, boxes of documents or files, rubbish bins and mobile drawers should not be stored under desks where they will decrease or interfere with the space required for the legs. Just remember that you’re at work to work, and whilst you may want to have a range of items on your desk, such items should not compromise your safety. Generally speaking, try not to place anything you regularly need to reach for out of comfortable reach. Large or heavy references should either be stored within close reach or in a nearby position where you stand up rather than reach awkwardly to access them.

topics.title: Keyboard and Mouse
topics.body: In relation to your keyboard, try tilting it using the feet at the back, to suit your level of comfort. A keyboard gel pad may be required where there’s an uncomfortable angle placed on the user’s wrist when using a keyboard or mouse. Place the keyboard and mouse as close to the front edge of the desk as is comfortable. Make sure that it is directly in front of you so you don’t have to twist towards it. Try not to place documents between the keyboard and the front edge of the desk while using the keyboard, as this increases the reach distance to the keyboard and may result in excessive bending of the neck to look at the documents. It’s best to place documents on a document holder beside your computer screen or for those big and bulky documents, place them on a document holder between your screen and the keyboard. Just make sure that it is at a comfortable height so you’re not looking down. Another good tip when using your mouse is to make sure your don’t keep your hand on your mouse when you aren’t using it. This tires out your hand and arm muscles. Give your hand a break and relax it when you can.

topics.title: Computer Screen & Notebook and Laptop Computers
topics.body:
Your computer screen should be positioned so that the top of the screen is level with or slightly lower than your eyes when you’re sitting upright and it should be placed approximately at arm’s length away from the usual seated position and placed in front of you to avoid glare or reflections from windows. If you use a notebook or laptop computer, you should use an external keyboard and mouse where possible and place the screen on a stand so that you use it like a normal computer screen. Whilst it may take a couple of minutes to set this up it’s certainly going to improve your posture and make things safer in the long run.

Occupational Violence - Handling Aggression

Finally, whilst it may not be relevant to every office worker, unfortunately we’re increasingly exposed to aggressive behaviour from others. Whether confronted with an aggressive client or customer, over the telephone or face to face, you need to know what to do. Remember these basic principles: Remain calm and respectful Use a low, calm tone of voice Listen - don’t intervene too quickly and allow the person to blow off steam Acknowledge the person’s feelings without diagnosis, encouragement or criticism Paraphrase and summarise what the person is saying by picking out the key points and repeating them out loud. Don’t debate the facts while the person is still angry, and When the person is sufficiently calm it is then appropriate to ask for details of and clarify the complaint or concern. You should not have to put up with this sort of behaviour unless you’re specifically employed to deal with such behaviour, but this would be rare. Once you’ve handled the situation, let the appropriate supervisor or employer representative know that they need to address it. But do it politely and be constructive.

topics.title: Emergency Management
topics.body: Fire, bomb threat, chemical exposure and personal assault can make you panic and act in a less than rational way and that’s why we practice getting evacuations and emergency management right. Know who your area warden is. That’s the person trained to tell you what to do and where to go in the event of an emergency. This person should be identified during your site and company specific induction prior to the commencement of work. Learn where the emergency stairs and evacuation points are for your building or floor. This may be shown on an emergency floor plan which should be displayed in your office. If you have an alarm system, know what each different alarm means. Find and memorise the location of fire extinguishers and manual alarms in your office. Learn where the emergency assembly points are, because this is where you need to go when you leave the building in an emergency and it’s critical that your area warden can account for you when you leave the building. Don’t use a lift unless your area warden says it’s safe to do so. Exit via the stairs where safe, and stay close to the handrail as this allows emergency officers to pass. If there’s smoke in the building remember to stay low and crawl to the emergency exit. If you’re confronted by an emergency try not to panic. I know it’s easy to say now, but panic doesn’t help anyone in an emergency. Follow the emergency management procedure if there’s one within your workplace. If there isn’t one provided in the site or company induction, follow it up with the responsible person.

topics.title: Threats
topics.body: Unfortunately, in today’s world there’s also the fear of bomb threats or something similar. Just remember, any threats that are received must be taken seriously, even if you don’t think they’re genuine. Your employer or other party responsible for your workplace safety should have a plan to deal with bomb threats or other threats such as terrorist threats. Given most threats are made by phone, a bomb or terrorist threat checklist should be kept near each telephone. A copy of this checklist should also be available within each work area in a generally accessible location given that threats can be received by email, fax or post. If you don’t have a bomb or terrorist threat checklist, you should ask your supervisor what the process should be in the event of receiving a threat and remind them that there should be an agreed procedure in place. Again, don’t wait until it happens because your capacity to move quickly or talk openly may be limited by the type of threat received.

topics.title: First Aid
topics.body: You’ll also need to know about first aid in the office, whether it’s in the event of an emergency or following an injury to you or someone around you. Remember, it’s not only a first aid officer that needs to know the basics of first aid and in some cases a first aid officer may not be available. You will need to know: How to contact your first aid officer; Where the first aid room or area is; Where first aid kits are located; What you will find in them; and What to do if you use something from the kit. These should all be covered off in your site and company specific safety induction and if they’re not, ask. In the event of a first aid emergency, a speedy and appropriate initial response can reduce discomfort and pain. But don’t rush things unnecessarily, that’s when others can get hurt in the process.

topics.title: Stress
topics.body: Did you know workplace stress is the second most common cause of workplace compensation claims in Australia after manual handling? Stress claims cost businesses $10.11 billion p.a. due to loss of productivity and absenteeism. This figure is likely to be under-represented however as it doesn’t include unsuccessful claims and those who do not make a formal claim. So what does stress actually mean? The World Health Organisation defines stress as “the reaction people may have when presented with demands and pressures that are not matched to their knowledge and abilities and which challenge their ability to cope”. Stress can occur in a wide range of situations, is complex and typically has multiple causes. Many jobs involve negative factors that put unwanted pressure (stress) on the worker, leading to adverse consequences. Stress is not a disease or injury in itself, but can lead to mental and physical ill health, and can also be a factor in workplace incidents.

topics.title: Negative Stress
topics.body: So, how is negative stress identified in the workplace? There are many different potential work-related stress hazards and risks in the workplace. You should be aware of systematic processes that the organisation undertakes to identify these hazards and risks. These processes should involve consultation with the workforce including you as a worker. Risks to psychological health in the workplace can largely be categorised as those relating to the social and physical work environment, the way that work is organised (system of work) and the way that work is managed. Some aspects of the social and physical environment that have the potential to cause harm are: role in the organisation career development, status and pay conflicting home/work demands physical work environment and equipment

topics.title: Stress and Systems of Work
topics.body: Issues relating to the way that work is organised (system of work) can include: the content and demands of the work the workload and pace of the work work schedules and working hours the extent of participation and control that people have over the work The way that work is managed can have harmful effects relating to: inadequate or unsupportive supervision lack of suitable information, instruction and training to enable employees to do their work

topics.title: Identifying & Managing Stress
topics.body: As a worker your employer owes you a duty of care. This duty of care extends to ensuring that your health and safety is not at risk; the meaning of health includes ‘psychological health’. Duty holders should be taking reasonable steps to eliminate or reduce the risk of negative stress. If you are a contractor, the on-hire/contracting firm can play a significant role in identifying and managing negative stress. Expect that your on-hire/contracting firm does the following: provides you with key job information (tasks, safety aspects, working hours including overtime, expected break times, remote work or working in isolation, reporting structure) maintains regular contact with you and offers opportunities to report any health and safety concerns associated with the contract assignment. For the Host, expect systems to manage the following areas: work environment systems of work work tasks If you feel you are exposed to negative stressors – report it to your supervisor/manager and (if appropriate) you’re on hire/contracting firm!

topics.title: Tips for dealing with Workplace Stress
topics.body:
You need to take some responsibility for identifying and managing stress, so here are some key points to consider:

Other Hazards in the Workplace

Many workplaces have a combination of operation; office, warehouse, manufacturing, maintenance areas and so on. Whilst your position and job tasks are predominately in the office, you may be exposed to other hazards in the workplace. For example; you may need to access the warehouse of your workplace to deliver or retrieve paperwork or consult with staff. This means you are exposed to the hazards in the warehouse; OR You may be working for a manufacturing business and whilst most of your time will be spent in the office, you may need to access the manufacturing area at intervals, exposing you to the hazards of the manufacturing work environment. It is important to be aware of your surroundings and risks that they present to your your health & safety. In addition to the hazards we have already considered in an office environment, there are additional hazards you should be aware of if you have to access these higher risk areas. The 3 most common of to these higher risks working environments are: Traffic Management Falling Objects Slips, Trips and Falls

topics.title: Slips, Trips and Falls
topics.body: (This step currently doesn't contain audio) The risk of slips, trips and falls are likely to be higher in warehouse and storage work environments. Warehouses may have water, oil, powders and/or other material on the floor such as plastic, labels etc. that may make the surface slippery. Good housekeeping is a great way to assist in managing the risk of a slip in these areas. For those who may only access these areas intermittently, it is important that appropriate footwear is worn. Poor lighting and obstructions may increase the risk of tripping in these work areas. Staying with pedestrian zones and walkways is the best way to prevent trips within warehouse and storage areas. At some point you may be required to access or retrieve an object, paperwork or material that has been stored at height. If so, it is important to be aware of safe access procedures. People can fall from step ladders. Under no circumstances should a domestic ladder be used in the workplace. Only use industrial rated ladders. Before you use a ladder, you should receive the appropriate information and instruction or training on its use. Where a ladder is used you must be able to show that it is not reasonably practicable to select an alternative, because the tasks is low risk and of short duration.

topics.title: Traffic Management
topics.body: There is no doubt, vehicles and pedestrians are not a good mix. It is very common for warehouse and storage facilities to have traffic moving in and around the work area. Serious injuries and death are frequently linked to mobile plant reversing as well as loading and unloading. The best way to control the risks associated with traffic in the workplace is to eliminate or isolate their interaction. Every workplace is different and the controls your workplace has in place to manage traffic may be different to other workplaces. Before you enter any areas at your workplace where there is traffic movement you should be familiar with the traffic management plan. Controls to assist in the management of traffic risks may include: Physical barriers, preventing pedestrians from accessing areas where mobile plant is operating Overhead walkways Pedestrian doors at vehicle entry and exit points Safety railing and /or bollards to prevent pedestrians stepping into blind spot traffic ares Interlocked gates, zoning and alarm systems Right of way procedures Site maps indicating traffic flow Personal protective equipment such as high visibility clothing and appropriate footwear Information, instruction and training on traffic management plans. The consequences of no or inadequate traffic management can be fatal. You should report any hazard to your supervisor immediately.

topics.title: Summary
topics.body: In finishing up I want to remind you that it’s critical that you take a proactive approach to workplace safety. When you wait for others to control risks in the workplace that’s when accidents occur. Remember the following essentials about office safety: Offices are not always safe; Complacency in offices contributes to injury and illness; Don’t wait for somebody else to fix the problem, be proactive, Don’t do work you haven’t been trained to do safely. Now, good luck with your assessment.

modules.description: This module outlines the risks and controls associated with a manufacturing environment:

topics.title: Introduction
topics.body: The manufacturing industry is very diverse. For example, it can cover the production of textiles, clothing and footwear, heavy machinery, food and beverages, chemicals and electronics. Some roles in manufacturing include: upholsterer machine operator plant operator textiles designer instrument fitter Because roles in a manufacturing environment are so varied, it is likely that you will need to undertake specific training to ensure your health and safety depending on the type of work that you are carrying out. This induction is only one part of preparing you to work safely and should be followed up with: A site-specific induction, and Specific work activity training that is delivered by your employer, principal, project manager or host organisation before you start working.

topics.title: Learning Outcomes

topics.title: Slips, Trips and Falls
topics.body: Slips and trips result in thousands of injuries every year. Slips occur when a person’s foot loses traction with the ground surface due to inappropriate footwear or slippery floor surfaces. Trips occur when a person catches their foot on an object or surface unexpectedly. Generally, most people trip on low obstacles that are not easily noticed such as uneven edges in flooring, loose matting, untidy equipment or cables. High risk areas include:

topics.title: What you can do to avoid Slips and Trips
topics.body:
Your employer should conduct regular workplace inspections; however, you can assist and reduce your risk of slips, trips and falls by paying close attention to the following:

Falls from Heights

You may be required to work at heights from time to time. Falls from heights presents a significant risk; workers have been seriously injured or killed when falling from heights as low as 1.5 metres. The bottom line is that it is unacceptable to work at heights without suitable fall protection. When it comes to working at any height remember the following: Remember the best control measure is elimination of the hazard, or redesign of the workplace environment. topics.title: Electrical Hazards
topics.body: Electrical injuries include shock, electrocution and electrical burns. Most accidents involving electricity results from either not isolating the electrical supply or working on live electrical equipment. Working with electricity can be particularly hazardous, especially when working in hostile conditions, such as: General precautions for working with electricity involve a combination of insulation, earthing and isolation. If you are working with, or around electricity in the above situations, you should be making sure that the electricity is isolated or locked out.

topics.title: Mobile Plant
topics.body: Most manufacturing environments require machinery, equipment and vehicles to move large and heavy items around; this is what we call ‘mobile plant’. One example of mobile plant is a forklift. Forklifts can cause significant injury or even fatalities when moving at a high speed or when they’re not being operated safely. You need to be aware of the things that can be done to minimise the likelihood of you being exposed to hazards associated with mobile plant. You play a very important role in identifying unsafe work practices and reporting them to your employer or other appropriate parties such as a Health and Safety Representative (if there is one).

topics.title: Controlling Mobile Plant Risks
topics.body:
Some of the things that can be done to reduce the likelihood of being exposed to hazards associated with mobile plant include:

Mobile Plant Operation

There’s no question that operators of mobile plant play a very important role in ensuring mobile plant safety. If you are operating, or working around mobile plant, you should be mindful of the following:

topics.title: Mobile Plant Stability
topics.body:
When operating or working around mobile plant you must be aware of the potential for it to overturn. Remember the following so as to prevent overturning of plant when operating, and to prevent being crushed by overturning mobile plant when you are in the vicinity of its operation:

Fixed Plant

Similar to mobile plant, fixed plant is a major cause of workplace death and injury. There are significant risks that come with using fixed plant, and unsafe use can result in injuries such as amputations, crushing injuries, fractures, hearing loss and electric shock. Hazardous fixed plant in manufacturing environments includes machinery with moving parts, such as:

Controlling the Risk of Fixed Plant

There is a large variety of types of fixed plant that you may come across in a manufacturing environment, and each should have their own specific controls to prevent injury. Just like other risks such as hazardous manual handling, the risks associated with fixed plant should be eliminated or minimized to reduce the likelihood of injury. The best, most robust controls, such as engineering, isolation and design measures should be in place where appropriate. These may include: emergency stops/warning devices, restricted access, or presence-sensing safeguarding. Appropriate PPE such as glasses, gloves and hearing protection are also important, as is ensuring you have appropriate and specific training for the plant you are using.

topics.title: Loading & Unloading Trucks
topics.body: Another particularly dangerous but necessary function in manufacturing is the loading and unloading of trucks.

topics.title: Hazardous Substances
topics.body: Many manufacturing environments require workers to work with or near chemicals and hazardous substances. Hazardous substances are substances that can harm the health of people using them. They can come in liquid, solid or gas form.

topics.title: First Aid
topics.body: You’ll also need to know about first aid in your workplace, whether it’s in the event of an emergency or following an injury to you or someone around you. Remember, it’s not only a first aid officer that needs to know the basics of first aid and in some cases a first aid officer may not be available. You will need to know: These should all be covered off in your site and company specific safety induction and if they’re not, ask. In the event of a first aid emergency, a speedy and appropriate initial response can reduce discomfort and pain.

topics.title: Negative Stress
topics.body: So, how is negative stress identified in the workplace? There are many different potential work-related stress hazards and risks in the workplace. You should be aware of systematic processes that the organisation undertakes to identify these hazards and risks. These processes should involve consultation with the workforce including you as a worker. Risks to psychological health in the workplace can largely be categorised as those relating to the social and physical work environment, the way that work is organised (system of work) and the way that work is managed. Some aspects of the social and physical environment that have the potential to cause harm are: role in the organisation career development, status and pay conflicting home/work demands physical work environment and equipment

topics.title: Stress and Systems of Work
topics.body: Issues relating to the way that work is organised (system of work) can include: the content and demands of the work the workload and pace of the work work schedules and working hours the extent of participation and control that people have over the work The way that work is managed can have harmful effects relating to: inadequate or unsupportive supervision lack of suitable information, instruction and training to enable employees to do their work

topics.title: Identifying & Managing Stress
topics.body: As a worker your employer owes you a duty of care. This duty of care extends to ensuring that your health and safety is not at risk; the meaning of health includes ‘psychological health’. Duty holders should be taking reasonable steps to eliminate or reduce the risk of negative stress. If you are a contractor, the on-hire/contracting firm can play a significant role in identifying and managing negative stress. Expect that your on-hire/contracting firm does the following: provides you with key job information (tasks, safety aspects, working hours including overtime, expected break times, remote work or working in isolation, reporting structure) maintains regular contact with you and offers opportunities to report any health and safety concerns associated with the contract assignment. For the Host, expect systems to manage the following areas: work environment systems of work work tasks If you feel you are exposed to negative stressors – report it to your supervisor/manager and (if appropriate) you’re on hire/contracting firm!
