topics.title: Introduction
topics.body: This module is a general safety induction for individuals working in and around a warehouse, distribution centre or stores area and is one element in preparing you to work safely. In addition to this module, you should receive: A site specific induction, and Specific work activity training that is delivered by your employer, principal, project manager or host organisation before you start working.

topics.title: Learning Outcomes
topics.body:
Once you’ve completed this module you should have a better understanding of the following:

Store Worker Hazards

Individuals working in and around stores/warehouses have a higher than average chance of being seriously injured at work. Almost 70% of these injuries are caused by hazardous manual handling and slips, trips and falls.

Typical Hazards and Risks

A hazard is anything that has the potential to cause injury or illness to you or damage to property around you. A risk is the likelihood and consequence of injury or illness arising from exposure to hazards. The most common hazards in a storage environment include the following: Hazardous manual handling, when picking, packing and undertaking other stores duties. This may include handling of heavy or awkward objects, or repetitive actions. The risks are made worse if these jobs are carried out over long periods, at a fast pace or in difficult conditions. Being struck by or crushed by mobile plant including forklifts and other vehicles. Slips and trips and falls from heights. Being struck by falling stock items. There certainly are others, but these are some of the most common factors contributing to injury within storage environments.

topics.title: Hazardous Manual Handling
topics.body: Manual handling involves much more than picking up and moving boxes. Any time that you need to use force to move, lift, push, pull, hold or carry an object is considered ‘manual handling’. So really, any interaction within the working environment involves Manual Handling. From a safety perspective, what we are interested in looking for is Hazardous Manual Handling. A task is deemed hazardous if it requires a person to lift, lower, push, pull, carry or otherwise move, hold or restrain any person, animal or thing that involves one or more of the followings: repetitive or sustained force high or sudden force repetitive movement sustained or awkward posture exposure to vibration In a stores environment, hazardous manual tasks may include: Lifting and/or carrying boxes or storage items. Moving items or equipment. Pushing or pulling trolleys.

topics.title: Minimising Hazardous Manual Handling
topics.body:
The risks associated with hazardous manual handling should be eliminated or minimized to reduce the likelihood of injury. For example, your workplace should ensure the design of the workplace, and/or equipment provided allows for employees to lift items from locations between shoulder and knee height. Safe Picking & Packing

Safe Lifting

It is vital that when you are in a workplace where you are constantly handling products and moving products, that you lift things safely. The first rule that we have is that if there is a trolley available or another form of mechanical aid then use them. If a trolley is not available make sure you adhere to the following safe lift principles:

Handling Pallets

Standard pallets, even when empty is heavy and awkward to manually handle. So remember, to manage risks associated with handling empty pallets it’s necessary to:

Slips, Trips and Falls

Slips and Trips Slips and trips result in thousands of injuries every year. Slips occur when a person’s foot loses traction with the ground surface due to inappropriate footwear or slippery floor surfaces. Trips occur when a person catches their foot on an object or surface unexpectedly. Generally, most people trip on low obstacles that are not easily noticed such as uneven edges in flooring, loose matting, untidy equipment or cables. High risk areas include:

What you can do to avoid Slips and Trips

Your employer should conduct regular workplace inspections; however, you can assist and reduce your risk of slips, trips and falls by paying close attention to the following:

Falls from Heights

You may be required to work at heights from time to time. Falls from heights present a significant risk; workers can be seriously injured or killed when falling from heights as low as 1.5 metres. The bottom line is that it is unacceptable to work at heights without suitable fall protection. When it comes to working at any height remember the following: Use appropriate equipment for gaining height above 1.8 metres. Use raised platforms in preference to ladders. Ladders are used to get to places, not to work from. If you are standing on a ladder, don’t stand higher than the second rung from the top. Don’t access areas of height without appropriate fall protection such as a harness. Remember the best control measure is elimination of the hazard, or redesign of the workplace environment or procedures such as slip resistant flooring, improved lighting or cleaning schedules. Administration controls such as training or signage should be seen as a last resort.

topics.title: Mobile Plant
topics.body: Most storage environments require machinery, equipment and vehicles to move large and heavy items around called mobile plant. One example of mobile plant is a forklift. Forklifts can cause significant injury or even fatalities when moving at a high speed or when they’re not being operated safely. You need to be aware of the things that can be done to minimise the likelihood of you being exposed to hazards associated with mobile plant. You play a very important role in identifying unsafe work practices and reporting them to your employer or other appropriate parties such as a Health and Safety Representative (if there is one at your workplace).

topics.title: Controlling Mobile Plant Risks
topics.body:
Some of the things that can be done to reduce the likelihood of being exposed to hazards associated with mobile plant include:

Mobile Plant Operation

There’s no question that operator’s of mobile plant play a very important role in ensuring mobile plant safety. If you are operating or working around mobile plant you should be mindful of the following;

Mobile Plant Stability

When operating or working around mobile plant you must be aware of the potential for it to overturn. Remember the following to prevent overturning of plant when operating, and to prevent being crushed by overturning mobile plant when you are in the vicinity of its operation:

Loading & Unloading Trucks

Another particularly dangerous but necessary function in stores is the loading and unloading of trucks.

Hazardous Substances

Many storage environments require individuals to work with or near chemicals and hazardous substances. Hazardous substances are substances that can harm the health of people using them. They come in liquid, solid or gas form. If these substances are inhaled, absorbed through the skin or swallowed you may suffer immediate or long-term effects to your health. It’s vitally important that hazardous substances are used and stored in the correct manner. The best way of determining correct use and storage is to obtain a copy of a document called a material safety data sheet or ‘MSDS’.

topics.title: Safe Storage & Handling of Dangerous Goods at the Workplace
topics.body: Dangerous goods are substances, mixtures or articles that, because of their properties, present an immediate hazard to people, property or the environment. They may be corrosive, flammable, combustible, explosive, oxidising or water-reactive or have other hazardous properties. There are nine classes of dangerous goods and these are represented by a diamond shaped warning sign identifying the principle hazard. The nine classes of dangerous goods are: Explosives Gases Flammable Liquids Flammable Solids Oxidising Substances Toxic & Infectious Substances Radioactive Material Corrosives Miscellaneous Dangerous Goods It is important to be familiar with dangerous goods classes as understanding the properties and hazards of each can affect the safe storage and handling of these substances. Where you identify signage that is obstructed or not easy to understand, you should report this to your supervisor for action.

topics.title: Signage & Placards
topics.body:
Safety signs in the workplace serve as reminders about the risks associated with dangerous goods and can assist with keeping people safe within the workplace. The following are common signs used in the workplace to assist with managing the risks associated with the storage and handling of dangerous goods:

Register/Manifest

Your workplace should have a register that identifies all dangerous goods stored and handled at the workplace. The register should be easily accessible to you as a worker and list the product names and be accompanied by a current SDS/MSDS for each of these dangerous goods. If your workplace has any dangerous goods that are in transit, you may not find these on the register as it is not a requirement.

MSDS's/SDS's

A Safety Data Sheet (SDS)/Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS), is a document that provides information on the properties of dangerous goods and how they affect health and safety in the workplace. For example, it includes information on the: identity, health and physicochemical hazards, safe handling and storage, emergency procedures, and disposal considerations of hazardous chemicals and their constituents. An SDS/MSDS is an important source of information that should be easily accessible to you at the workplace. Before storing or handling any dangerous goods you should review and consider the information within the SDS/MSDS, this process will assist with managing the risk of the dangerous good. If an SDS/MSDS is not available for a dangerous good in the workplace, you should report this immediately to your supervisor and not interact with the dangerous good until you receive adequate information regarding the safe storage handling.

topics.title: Information, instruction, training and supervision
topics.body: It is expected that all workers involved in the storage and handling of dangerous goods are provided with adequate information, instruction, training and supervision. Specifically, as a worker your induction, information and training provided by your employer should include instruction on: nature of the hazards and properties of the dangerous goods and the processes used for the identification and control of the risks associated with the person’s tasks purpose, use and maintenance of the measures for the control of those risks systems of work and the conduct of persons at the premises to the extent this affects the safe storage and handling of dangerous goods operation of the emergency plan for the premises and any procedures and equipment that may be required for use in the event of an emergency, and proper use and fitting of personal protective equipment (PPE). If you have not received adequate information, instruction training and supervision on the safe storage and handling of dangerous goods at your workplace, report to and consult with your supervisor.

topics.title: Risk Management
topics.body: Although the risk management of dangerous goods in the workplace ultimately lies with the employer/occupier, workers play a key role in identifying, assessing, controlling and reviewing risk control strategies. The eyes, ears and voices of workers are crucial aspect of managing the risks associated with the storage and handling of dangerous goods in the workplace. Identification: task/workplace observation, reviewing labels and SDS/MSDS and consulting with colleagues, managers and even suppliers are great ways to identify hazards associated with the storage and handling of dangerous goods. Assessment: risk assessments are not a legislative requirement however it may be a practice adopted by your workplace to assist in managing the risk of dangerous goods, therefore your cooperation and participation in the risk assessment process is invaluable. Controls: the best way to control hazards are to eliminate them, however this is not always practical. Suggestions for ways to eliminate or significantly reduce the risk by substitution, isolation, administration and PPE controls should be reported through to your management team to assist them in complying with their duty of care towards you and your colleagues. Review: where a control has been implemented and is no longer suitable, it is important that you report this to management and if possible suggest alternative controls that may be more suitable to the risk.

topics.title: PPE
topics.body: As you may be aware personal protective equipment (PPE) is the least preferred control in the hierarchy of controls, this is because it relies on human behaviour to manage the risk. PPE can however be a great control when it is used in combination with higher level controls, and therefore PPE may be used as a way to assist in managing the risks associated with the storage and handling of dangerous goods. It is important to refer to the SDS/MSDS before handling dangerous goods as the SDS/MSDS identifies the suggested PPE to be worn

topics.title: Segregation
topics.body: Some dangerous goods classes are not compatible with other classes of dangerous goods. As a result, there are segregation requirements that you must be familiar with and keep in mind at all times when storing and handling dangerous goods in the workplace.

topics.title: Transfer of DG's
topics.body:
The transfer of dangerous goods refers to any process that involves: filling, loading, pumping or pouring of dangerous goods into a container, or discharging, unloading, pumping or pouring of dangerous goods from a container. When transferring dangerous goods in the workplace, you should consider the following factors to assist with risk management:

Stability

Many dangerous goods are highly reactive, unstable or self-reactive except under controlled conditions. It is important that you are familiar with and follow your workplace procedures to ensure controlled conditions are maintained. Information regarding stability of dangerous goods can be found in the SDS/MSDS of each product. Anytime you identify dangerous goods becoming unstable, decomposing or changing in any way that introduces a new hazard and risk or increases an existing risk, you should report it immediately to management.

topics.title: Access and Security
topics.body: Access and security are an important consideration for workplaces when identifying suitable controls for the storage and handling of dangerous goods. Your workplace may have various security measures in place to prevent access to the worksite by unauthorised persons. Controls such as locks on doors and windows, fencing or enclosed areas, alarm systems, security checks and CCTV are examples of security measures to assist with unauthorised access to dangerous goods storage areas. You should be provided with information on the security systems and procedures to ensure these are effectively used and implemented.

topics.title: Spill Containment
topics.body: The storage and handling of dangerous goods at the workplace presents a risk of spill. SDS/MSDS identify the requirements for spill containment and clean-up for each product. In addition to the information provided in the SDS/MSDS, your workplace procedures should identify a process for spill containment. Your workplace may have various forms of spill containment, these may include: drains to a purpose built on-site catchment surface grading so that all spills are contained by the contours bunding the area to form a compound double-walled containers, or enclosing a tank with a partial or full-height bund; and spill kits It is important that you are familiar with and follow any procedures in place to manage dangerous goods spills at the workplace.

topics.title: Dangerous occurrences and reporting incidents
topics.body: If you experience or observe an incident involving dangerous goods, it is important that you report it to management immediately. Early reporting of the following incidents is crucial, as your employer/occupier of the premises has a duty to notify emergency services: a person is injured or exposed to an immediate risk to health or safety as a result of the incident, at the workplace or an adjacent premises there is damage to property as a result of the incident, at the workplace or an adjacent premises there is potential for the incident to escalate in seriousness and endanger or injure a person or damage property, at your premises or an adjacent premises the incident may lead to environmental damage beyond the workplace premises

modules.title: Contact Centre Worker Safety
modules.description: This module outlines risks and controls, and office safety procedures and requirements. It includes:

topics.title: Welcome
topics.body: Welcome to your work safety induction. Before you get started, there are a few things we need to share with you: This module will take about 30 minutes to complete, not including the assessment You can progress at your own pace using the 'NEXT' and 'BACK' buttons. This module includes audio. If you don't have time to complete all the module in one sitting, the next time you log in you will automatically be presented with the last step you were on. Once you have completed the module: An email will be sent to the requesting organisation. An email will be sent to you for your records. All current modules will be displayed in your online profile.

topics.title: Introduction
topics.body: You are about to complete the Call Centre worker safety induction module. Call Centre’s are often referred to as Contact Centre’s, but for the purposes of this module, this term will commonly be referred to as Call Centre. This safety induction module covers general information for workers working in a Call Centre environment. Remember though that this safety induction is only one part of preparing you to work safely and should be followed up with; 1. A site specific induction, and 2. Specific work activity training that is delivered by your employer, principal, project manager or host organisation before you start working.

topics.title: Learning Outcomes
topics.body: Once you’ve completed this safety induction you should have a better understanding of the following: The most common hazards and risks in a Call Centre environment What you can do to prevent these risks injuring someone or making them ill, and Some broader safe work principles Because this induction focuses on general Call Centre worker safety, it doesn’t cover everything. There are other induction modules and training courses available in the library that cover these areas, and you may be requested to complete other courses in addition to this module.

topics.title: General Information about Call Centres
topics.body: Call Centre’s are recognised as one of the fastest growing workplaces in Australia. A Call Centre is a central or distributed contact point where customer contacts are managed. Generally, Call Centre’s provide product support and information to customers by telephone as well as other means of communication e.g. fax, email. Call Centre’s are generally perceived safe as it is work in an office, however the work environment and organisation of a Call Centre presents a range of hazards that can result in injury and illness. Some of the most persistent injuries have arisen in Call Centre environments either as a result of the environment or because of the type of work being done.

topics.title: Common Call Centre Hazards
topics.body: A hazard is anything that has the potential to cause injury or illness to you or damage to property around you. A risk is the likelihood of injury or illness arising from exposure to these hazards. Like many work environments, call centres have specific hazards, however many of the hazards that exist in call centres are common in other work environments, these hazards include: manual tasks ergonomics - workstation design stress occupational violence emergencies Some of the hazards that are more specific to call centres are: acoustic incidents and background noise visual discomfort voice fatigue headset hygiene Let's explore these hazards in more detail.

topics.title: Acoustic Incidents & Background Noise
topics.body: Firstly, acoustic incidents and background noise. Acoustic incidents are sudden, unexpected loud noises occurring through a receiver during telephone or headset use. They may be crackles, hisses, whistles or shrieks or high-pitched noises. The sources of acoustic noise from the transmission system can be: faulty or damaged networks, telephones and headset equipment; broadband and narrowband interference; and mobile phones or fax machines used in call centres As the person on the receiving end of the call you may experience the following: feedback oscillation from some cordless phones; alarm signals; signalling tones; phone receivers slammed down or dropped; tones from misdirected facsimiles and modems; and noises made close to the receiver, such as people whistling and babies screaming. Acoustic incidents are very common in a Call Centre environment but a small number of these do result in acoustic shock. Background noises at the workplace can also increase the risk of acoustic shock.

topics.title: Acoustic Shock
topics.body: Acoustic shock are the symptoms you may experience as a result of an acoustic incident. Acoustic shock is not a result of the loudness of the noise; it is the sudden rise in noise levels. There are three levels of symptoms a person can experience from an acoustic incident: Primary Secondary Tertiary Primary symptoms are immediate and can include dizziness, tinnitus, nausea and vomiting, a feeling of numbness, soreness and/or tingling on the face, neck or shoulder. There is the possibility of hearing loss, however this is rare. Headaches, fatigue, vertigo and anxiety are secondary symptoms, whilst sensitivity to sounds and being overly alert are tertiary symptoms of acoustic shock.

topics.title: Managing Acoustic Shock
topics.body:
To manage risks associated with acoustic incidents: Check loud or high-pitched noises by notifying your team leader, supervisor or other persons responsible for technical issues in the Call Centre. Notify your team leader or supervisor of damaged equipment or network faults. Ensure your headset is properly maintained. Reduce background noises as far as possible. If the problem persists, you may require a headset with an acoustic shock prevention device.

Visual Discomfort

It can be generalised that the work carried out by Call Centre workers involves the intensive use of computer screens. The health effects of intensive use of computer screens, commonly referred to as VDUs (visual display units) is the short-term effect on the eyes. These short-term effects can present in the form of sore eyes, blurred vision, tired eyes and headaches. To ensure visual comfort whilst at work, the following should be practiced: adjust screen to the correct height keep screen from glare and reflections by controlling ambient light conditions keep screen clean manage the font to a size that is comfortable to view position reference material in close promixity allow for visual breaks, this may be changes in activity to assist in preventing visual fatigue if you feel that the lighting levels are inadequate report to your Manager/Supervisor to have the luminance measured.

topics.title: Voice Fatigue
topics.body: As a Call Centre worker, you may be required to talk excessively, this can lead to overuse and voice strain. The symptoms of voice strain include: loss of voice pain and tension loss of pitch or expression croakiness, or an irritating cough difficulties breathing and swallowing To manage risks associated with vocal fatigue in Call Centres: shorten open greeting scripts where possible take adequate rest breaks reduce background noise adjust volume control on the headset so that voice does not need to be raised drink water to regularly perform non-speaking tasks until your vocal fatigue subsides, where possible training on headset use; positioning of microphone and volume controls There is actually a correct way to position a microphone on your headset to ensure customers can hear you speak and that means you avoid vocal fatigue and the capture of unnecessary background noise. Ask your team leader, supervisor or other Call Centre representative to show you where the best position for your microphone is, as it may change from one headset to another.

topics.title: Headset Hygiene
topics.body: Without proper hygiene, the sharing of headsets can spread respiratory and other infections such as ‘tropical ear’. You should be provided with your own headset with fresh ear piece covers or sterile ear pads. It’s also a good idea to use sterile wipes to clean the ear and mouth piece in line with operating instructions every shift. Instructions for cleaning on a regular basis should be provided to you. As headsets are usually worn throughout a shift, they should be fully adjustable to ensure your comfort. Headsets should be checked regularly and repaired immediately if necessary. Given this is a piece of equipment central to your work you have a right to suitable equipment.

topics.title: Workstation Design
topics.body: Call Centre workers spend virtually all of their work time within their workstations, so it's no surprise that many of the hazards a Call Centre worker is exposed to are a result of the workstation design. There are many things about workstations that can lead to musculoskeletal disorders. Consider the characteristics of a Call Centre workstation: hot-desks (worker works at a different workstation each shift) sitting at the workstation for long durations limited autonomy repetitive movements: keyboard and mouse use There are practical ways to manage workstation related hazards.

topics.title: Hot Desks
topics.body: As these workstations may be used by various workers on a shift to shift basis the workstations provided by the employer should be adjustable. If you are hot-desking at your workplace, it is important that you adjust your workstation to suit the task demands, your body dimensions and personal needs. Allow yourself adequate time at the start of your shift to make adjustments to your furniture before you start working! As a reminder to adjust your workstation it's a good idea to set up screen prompts that alert you at the start of each shift.

topics.title: Reducing the risk of MSD
topics.body: To reduce the risk of MSD from workstation design and activity consult with your manager and health and safety representative about ways in which tasks can be varied to limit the amount of time sitting at the workstation; number an duration of breaks; provide for autonomy and to reduce repetitive movements. Some factors to consider when consulting with management and your health and safety representative on ways to reduce the risk of MSD: It is important to include task variety in the design of work. This can be achieved by mixing intensive keyboard use and other computer use with a variety of other work. It is important that the different tasks involve a change in posture and muscles used to perform the work. As the working day progresses it becomes more important to provide work with different mental demands, changes in posture and more frequent work breaks. It is important for your workplace to provide information on how to vary tasks and postures throughout the day. As important as it is to reduce the risks associated with the workstation and repetitive tasks; it is just as important to set up your chair correctly as well as other components of your work area... here's how:

topics.title: Chair Height
topics.body: Firstly, adjust your chair height so your feet are comfortably flat on the floor, your thighs are horizontal and your lower legs vertical. Just think of a ninety-degree angle at your knees. Remember that low heeled shoes will improve comfort of the legs with the chair at this height If your seat is tilt adjustable, set it to horizontal initially, although you may wish to adjust the tilt slightly forward to suit your comfort.

topics.title: Chair Backrest
topics.body: Start by raising the backrest to its maximum height. Then sit in the chair and check the fit of the back rest to the curve of the lower back. If not comfortable, lower the height accordingly. Adjust the position of the back rest forward or back until a comfortable pressure is exerted on the low back area while seated in the usual working posture at the desk. The back-rest position should not feel as though it pushes you out of the seat or that you have to lean too far back to reach it. There should be a two-finger clearance between the front of the chair and the back of the knee.

topics.title: Chair Arm Rests & Desk Height
topics.body: Arm rests on a chair are not a great idea so if you have them you should ask about removing them. This is because they can prevent you getting close enough to the desk and can make you bend forward to reach things. Now that you’ve adjusted your chair let’s take a look at your desk. If you have a height-adjustable desk, adjust its height so that the top of the surface is just below elbow height. If you don’t have a height-adjustable desk don’t stress, there are other things you can do. If your desk is too high raise your chair by the required distance and use a foot rest. Set the foot rest platform so that it is the same as the measured distance so that your body and posture is not compromised. or Lower the desk, if you’re allowed, by reducing the leg length by the measured difference. If the desk is too low, raise the height of the desk by extending the leg length or sitting it on wooden blocks or something similar. Remember to ensure that any such changes are secure and stable.

topics.title: Under Desks
topics.body: It’s important not to clutter underneath your desk because this will limit your ability to work naturally and avoid adopting a twisted or awkward posture of the spine. General items, such as computer hard disk drives, boxes of documents or files, rubbish bins and mobile drawers should not be stored under desks where they will decrease or interfere with the space required for the legs.

topics.title: Storage on Top of Desks
topics.body: Just remember that you’re at work to work, and whilst you may want to have a range of items on your desk such items should not compromise your safety. Generally speaking, try not to place anything you regularly need to reach for out of comfortable reach. Large or heavy references should either be stored within close reach or in a nearby position where you stand up rather than reach awkwardly to access them.

topics.title: Keyboard and Mouse
topics.body: In relation to your keyboard, try tilting it using the feet at the back, to suit your level of comfort. A keyboard gel pad may be required where there’s an uncomfortable angle placed on the user’s wrist when using a keyboard or mouse. Place the keyboard and mouse as close to the front edge of the desk as is comfortable. Make sure that it is directly in front of you so you don’t have to twist towards it. Try not to place documents between the keyboard and the front edge of the desk while using the keyboard. Its best to place documents on a document holder beside your computer screen or for those big and bulky documents, place them on a document holder between your screen and the keyboard. Just make sure that it is at a comfortable height so you’re not looking down. Another good tip when using your mouse is to make sure that you don’t keep your hand on your mouse when you aren’t using it.

topics.title: Computer Screen
topics.body:
Your computer screen should be positioned so that the top of the screen is level with or slightly lower than your eyes when you’re sitting upright. Your screen should be placed approximately at arm’s length away from the usual seated position and placed in front of you to avoid glare or reflections from windows.

Stress

Did you know workplace stress is the second most common cause of workplace compensation claims in Australia after manual handling? Stress claims cost businesses $10.11 billion p.a. due to loss of productivity and absenteeism. This figure is likely to be under-represented however as it doesn’t include unsuccessful claims and those who do not make a formal claim. So what does stress actually mean? The World Health Organisation defines stress as “the reaction people may have when presented with demands and pressures that are not matched to their knowledge and abilities and which challenge their ability to cope”. Many jobs involve negative factors that put unwanted pressure (stress) on the worker, leading to adverse consequences. Stress is not a disease or injury in itself, but can lead to mental and physical ill health, and can also be a factor in workplace incidents.

topics.title: Negative Stress
topics.body: So, how is negative stress identified in the workplace? There are many different potential work-related stress hazards and risks in the workplace. You should be aware of systematic processes that the organisation undertakes to identify these hazards and risks. These processes should involve consultation with the workforce including you as a worker. Risks to psychological health in the workplace can largely be categorised as those relating to the social and physical work environment, the way that work is organised (system of work) and the way that work is managed. Some aspects of the social and physical environment that have the potential to cause harm are: role in the organisation career development, status and pay conflicting home/work demands physical work environment and equipment

topics.title: Emergency Management
topics.body: The consequence of poor or non-existent emergency management procedures and processes is significant. Fire Bomb threat Chemical exposure, and Personal assault

topics.title: Emergency Management (continued)
topics.body:
Remember the following about emergency management in a Call Centre: Know who your area warden is. This is the person who has been formally trained to tell you what to do, and where to go in the event of an emergency. This person should be identified during your site and company specific induction prior to the commencement of work. Learn where the emergency stairs and evacuation points are for your building or floor. This may be shown on an emergency floor plan which should be displayed in your Call Centre. If you have an alarm system, know what each different alarm means. Find and memorise the location of fire extinguishers and manual alarms in your Call Centre. Learn where the emergency assembly points are. This is where you need to go when you leave the building in an emergency and it’s critical that your area warden can account for you when you leave the building. Don’t use a lift unless your area warden says it’s safe to do so. Exit via the stairs where safe, and stay close to the handrail as this allows emergency officer’s to pass. If there’s smoke in the building remember to stay low and crawl to the emergency exit. If you’re confronted by an emergency try not to panic. Follow the emergency management procedure if there’s one within your workplace. If there isn’t one provided in the site or company induction, follow it up with the responsible person.

Threats

In Call Centre environments, there is a very real fear of bomb threats or something similar. Just remember, any threats that are received must be taken seriously, even if you don’t think they’re genuine. Your employer or other party responsible for your workplace safety should have a plan to deal with bomb threats or other threats such as terrorist threats. Given most threats are made by phone, a bomb or terrorist threat checklist should be kept near each telephone. A copy of this checklist should also be available within each work area in a generally accessible location given that threats can be received by email, fax or post. If you don’t have a bomb or terrorist threat checklist, you should ask your supervisor what the process should be in the event of receiving a threat and remind them that there should be an agreed procedure in place. Don’t wait until something happens because your capacity to move quickly or talk openly may be limited by the type of threat received.

topics.title: First Aid
topics.body: You need to know about first aid in a Call Centre, whether it’s in the event of an emergency or following an injury to you or someone around you. Remember, it’s not only a First Aid Officer who needs to know the basics of first aid and in some cases a First Aid Officer may not be available. You need to know the following about first aid: How to contact your first aid call officer; Where the first aid room or area is; Where first aid kits are located; What you will find in them; and What to do if you use something from the kit. These should all be covered off in your site and company specific safety induction and if they’re not, ask. In the event of a first aid emergency, a speedy and appropriate initial response can reduce discomfort and pain.

topics.title: General Fatigue
topics.body:
Fatigue is a general term used to describe the feeling of being tired, drained or exhausted. Fatigue is accompanied by poor judgment, slower reactions to events and decreased skills. Fatigue can be more common in Call Centre environments where there is little variety or diversity or where you are working regular afternoon or night shifts. To manage risks associated with fatigue: Ask for a revision of your roster to allow you sufficient good quality sleep of at least six hours, taken in a single continuous period. Ensure you get at least 24 hours notice before night work. Ensure you have a regular and familiar roster. Consider alternatives to night shifts where suitable.

House Keeping

Some of the fundamentals of Call Centre housekeeping are as follows: Maintain a clean and tidy work area; Don’t run leads across hallways and pedestrian traffic areas; Walk cautiously and slowly when approaching blind corners, especially when carrying objects; Make sure emergency exits are not blocked by storage items or by waste and rubbish; Place paper and cardboard waste into the suitable bin for recycling; Ensure power boards are not overloaded; Don’t overload shelves or cupboards; Don’t place heaters too close to walls or in confined areas where they might overheat; and Turn off electrical appliances at the end of the day.

Equipment

Equipment includes everything from cutting implements to photocopiers, fax machines, Call Centre furniture and workstation equipment. Equipment which is used in the wrong way or poorly maintained can lead to accidental injury. So make sure you get proper instruction on how to use equipment and don’t presume all equipment is the same. In the best Call Centre environments there should be safe operating procedures available to assist with training and safe use. Don’t be afraid to ask for them and if there are no procedures available, consult the instruction booklet that came with the equipment.

topics.title: Electrical Devices & Attachments
topics.body:
Electricity can kill and non-fatal accidents can cause permanent injury. Poor electrical installations may also lead to fires, so make sure you: Switch off and disconnect electrical appliances that seem faulty. They must be reported and repaired or replaced. Make sure you keep electrical devices and attachments well away from water. Water is typically found in kitchens, bathrooms and drinking cups in Call Centres, so don’t put power boards, double adaptors or other devices in kitchens and bathrooms, be aware of where you leave glasses and mugs.

Slips & Trips

Slips, trips and fall hazards are a major source of office incidents and injuries! Slippery floor surfaces are a hazard and often cause a slip when someone walks on it. This can be avoided easily by the prompt clean-up of spilled materials. Inappropriate footwear is also a contributing factor to incidents involving a slip. Obstructions and uneven surfaces are primary trip hazards and these can be avoided by ensuring that floor surfaces are clear and even. So, how do we fall in the office? ... This is usually a result of standing on chairs or shelves to reach upper storage levels. Falls can also occur on poorly designed or badly lit stairwells or worn stair edges. What type of injuries can be sustained from slips, trips and falls? Slips, trips and falls result in thousands of injuries every year. Most common are musculoskeletal injuries, as well as cuts, bruises, fractures and dislocations. Some of the ways you can manage the risk of slips, trips & falls are: prompt cleaning of spilled materials; use of ‘slippery when wet’ signage; appropriate footwear; regular housekeeping inspections are reported; regular cleaning and maintenance program; provide and use handrails or guardrails on all platforms, steps or stairs; secure carpets and rugs, and remove any flooring that “lifts”; secure slip-resistant doormats at entrances or ensure that they are large enough to remain in place.

Chemicals & Other Hazardous Substances

Chemicals and other hazardous substances are more common in a Call Centre than you think. Cleaning products are a great example. Chemicals and other agents in a Call Centre have the potential to harm you, your work mates and visitors to the Call Centre. Remember, they can be in liquid as well as gas form. It’s not just about you, it’s about everyone in a Call Centre. Keep hazardous substances locked away in appropriate storage, so that even if the substances leak others won’t be exposed to them. Remember that means prevention of leakage into the air as well as onto the floor.

topics.title: Hazardous Substances and the MSDS/SDS
topics.body: Read warning labels on containers and follow manufacturer’s instructions in relation to storage. If you come into contact with or breathe in a hazardous substance, get a copy of the Material Safety Data Sheet/Safety Data Sheet, which will tell you how to handle the exposure. A material safety data sheet/safety data sheet is a guide provided by manufacturers that outlines everything from how dangerous something is through to what to do if you are exposed to the substance. They’re called an MSDS or SDS and should be available near all chemicals and substances in the Call Centre.

topics.title: Storage
topics.body: Given we’re constantly referring to written material and other items in Call Centres, the way things are stored is very important. A lot of injuries occur because of unnatural bending, lifting and twisting. Suitable storage of materials in a Call Centre will minimise the risk of accidents occurring. When filing or storing, the most commonly used items should be placed according to bulk and weight in readily accessible areas between knee and shoulder height. Don’t put heavy items up high because it will put extra strain on you when you try to get them down again, not to mention the likelihood of them dropping on top of you.

topics.title: Safe Lifting
topics.body:
Perform safe lifting techniques, as follows: Plan the lift. Position yourself over the load. Bend your knees to get in the correct position to lift with your legs, not your back. Take a secure grip. Pull and keep the load in close to the body. Lift it smoothly whilst keeping your back straight and your head looking forward.

Occupational Violence - Handling Aggression

Whilst it may not be relevant to every Call Centre worker, workers can be exposed to aggressive behaviour. When confronted with an aggressive client or customer on the telephone, there are some fundamental things to remember, including: Remain calm and respectful. Use a low, calm tone of voice. Listen - don’t intervene too quickly and allow the person to voice their opinion and view. Acknowledge the person’s feelings without diagnosis, encouragement or criticism. Paraphrase and summarise what the person is saying by picking out the key points and repeating them out loud. Don’t debate the facts while the person is still angry. When the person is sufficiently calm it is then appropriate to ask for details of and clarify the complaint or concern. Remember that there comes a point in every call where it may be appropriate to terminate the call if an individual does not calm down. Once you’ve handled the situation, let your team leader, the appropriate supervisor or employer representative know that they need to address it. But do it politely and be constructive. After an abusive call, it may be a good idea to ask your team leader if you can take a short break before moving to the next call.

topics.title: Summary
topics.body:
Remember the following essentials about Call Centre safety. Call Centres are not always safe. Complacency in Call Centres contributes to injury and illness. Don’t wait for somebody else to fix the problem, be proactive. Don’t do work you haven’t been trained to do safely. Communicate with your Supervisor, team leader and manager, and report incident and hazards to ensure that the risk is minimised and/or removed.

Completion of Learning Section

To finalise the training, it is necessary to undertake a short assessment to ensure you have a good understanding of the module content. The assessment involves answering a number of multiple choice and true/false questions. In order to pass this assessment, you will need to answer 80% of the questions correctly. If you do not meet the required pass rate, you will be presented with a new series of questions. Once you have successfully completed the assessment, you will be provided with a Candidate Identification Number (CIN) and PIN. This, along with details of the course completed will be emailed to your registered email address.

topics.title: Overview of Work Health & Safety (WHS)
topics.body: Your Employer’s Duty of Care Work health and safety law places a primary duty of care on the employer/person conducting the business or undertaking (PCBU). By law, the organisation you work for is deemed the employer/PCBU therefore they must ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, your health and safety while you are at work. In order to achieve this, your organisation is required to protect the health and safety of yourself, your colleagues and others who may be exposed to the risks of the organisation by eliminating risks to health and safety. If this is not reasonably practicable, risks must be minimised so far as is reasonably practicable. Your Safety Obligation Whilst in your nursing role, you are deemed a worker. Worker's duty under work health and safety law requires you to take reasonable care for your own health and safety and that of others who may be affected by your actions or omissions. You must also: comply, so far as you are reasonably able, with any reasonable instruction given by the organisation to allow the organisation to comply with WHS laws, and cooperate with any reasonable policy or procedure of the organisation relating to health or safety at the workplace that has been notified to you. Assessment Task As a worker which of the following IS true regarding your responsibilities for work health and safety: a) It is not necessary for you to cooperate with any reasonable policy or procedure of the organisation relating to health or safety at the workplace that has been notified to workers. b) You must comply, so far as reasonably practicable, with any reasonable instruction given by the organisation to allow the organisation to comply with WHS laws c) Safe Work Practices do not need to be adhered to. d) You, as a worker, do not need to be familiar with work health and safety procedures. Which of the following strategies would NOT assist in reducing stress levels? a) Scheduling work meetings out of work hours. b) Restricting overtime hours. c) Use annual leave each year and ensure you are taking a proper break from work. d) Identifying people such as close friends or counsellors who you can talk to obtain support. topics.title: Hazardous Manual Tasks
topics.body:
From a safety perspective, what we are interested in looking for is those manual tasks that are ‘hazardous’. Hazardous manual tasks are not just those tasks that involve heavy lifting. For example: Lifting and/or carrying boxes, equipment and products and storage items. Repetitive activities such as unpacking pallets, stacking shelves, scanning and pricing. Moving items or equipment. Pushing, pulling and maneuvering trolleys. Any time you undertake a task where you carry or otherwise move, lift, lower, push, pull, hold or restrain an object that involves one or more of the following is considered a hazardous manual task: repetitive or sustained force high or sudden force repetitive movement sustained or awkward posture exposure to vibration. These are known as characteristics of a hazardous manual task. They directly stress the body and can lead to injury.

Taking the ‘Hazardous’ out of Manual Tasks

There are many ways in which a manual task can be altered so that it is no longer hazardous. Before undertaking a manual task in your workplace consider if there is anything you can do to reduce the risk: Elimination - does the task need to be done manually? Is there another way the task can be done that removes the manual factor? Substitution - are there alternative control measures? e.g. rather than overloading the small trolley to move your load, is there another type of trolley that is available that is larger, easy to move and securely carries the load? Engineering - are there mechanical aids available in the workplace that are intended to be used for manual tasks? E.g. height adjustable trolley’s, height adjustable workstations, lifting hoists, electric pallet jacks etc. Pushing vs Pulling - it is important to remember that pushing loads is preferable to pulling because it involves less work by the muscles of the lower back, allows maximum use of body weight, less awkward postures and generally allows workers to adopt a forward-facing posture, providing better vision in the direction of travel. Administrative - can you organise the work to minimise multiple handling and improve the flow of work? E.g. requesting couriers to deliver stock to the stock room rather than on the shop floor. Can the risk be minimised by sharing the task through job rotation? Is there an opportunity for rest breaks in between repetitive tasks? Is there an option for team handling? Check with your manager what information, instruction and training is available in the workplace to assist with managing the risk of hazardous manual tasks

topics.title: Falls
topics.body: The risk of a fall in retail is high. "Risk of Fall" means a situation that exposes a worker or other person at or in the vicinity of the workplace to a risk of a fall that is likely to cause an injury. In the retail work environment fall risk situations may include a person: in or on plant or a structure that is at an elevated level in or on plant that is being used to gain access to an elevated level in the vicinity of an opening through which a person could fall in the vicinity of an edge over which a person could fall on or in the vicinity of a surface through which a person could fall on or near the vicinity of a slippery, sloping or unstable surface. It’s important to analyse the task and identify fall risks prior to carrying out the task. Some tasks that should be of particular focus and concern include those tasks that are carried out: with the aid of elevated work equipment such as elevating work platforms and portable ladders on an unstable or potentially unstable and/or fragile surface on a structure or plant that is being constructed, repaired, cleaned etc. on slippery surfaces on an unprotected edge or near a hole

topics.title: Controlling the fall risk in retail
topics.body: Managing the risk of fall in retail requires analysis of the task and careful consideration on adequate and practical control measures. For any task presenting the risk of fall, consider the following: Can the need to work at height be avoided to eliminate the risk of a fall? Can the fall be prevented by working on solid construction? Can the risk of a fall be minimised by providing and maintaining a safe system of work, including installation of guard rails, work positioning systems, harness systems etc. In some cases a combination of control measures may be necessary, for example using a safety harness while working from an elevating work platform. Safe work procedures, information, instruction, training and supervision are additional controls that should be combined with higher level controls in the effort to control the risk of fall.

topics.title: Falls from Ladders
topics.body: Ladders are a particular concern in the retail environment. It is reported that retail sales assistants are the third highest occupation group that suffers serious injuries as a result of falls from ladders. In retail, limited space is a big factor when selecting and using ladders. Unfortunately, in many situations the work around for limited space means opting for small domestic ladder to get the job done. While domestic ladders are cost effective and portable, they pose a real risk for retailer workers. For example, if such ladders do not suit the task, the worker may over-stretch and fall. In other cases, the ladder’s specifications may not meet the load the worker is bearing, causing falls as a result of broken rungs.

topics.title: Slips and Trips
topics.body: One of the most common causes of injury within the retail industry is when a worker or customer slips or trips. Slippery surfaces in the retail industry can be found in places such as cool rooms, freezers, deli areas, meat rooms, bakery areas, food preparation areas, storage areas and any area where moist products and liquids are likely to be spilled. topics.title: Preventing Slips and Trips in the Workplaces
topics.body: So here are some tips on how to prevent slips and trips in retail work:

topics.title: Fatigue
topics.body:
Fatigue can be a result of work-related factors and/or factors outside work, which may accumulate over time. Some examples of factors that can lead to fatigue are: lengths of shifts poor work scheduling and planning length of time worked inadequate rest breaks There can be short term effects of fatigue, these can include but are not limited to: reduced ability to make decisions; think laterally and analytically; concentrate and recognise risks. Longer term affects can include but are not limited to: depression, anxiety and heart disease; these health effects are usually associated with shift work and chronic sleep loss. Fatigue can also increase the likelihood of incidents and injuries!

Reducing Fatigue

Some simple measures can significantly reduce the risk of fatigue. These include but are not limited to: use of rest periods (in addition to meal breaks) introduce job rotation redesign the job to include a variety of tasks avoid working arrangements that provide incentives to work excessive hours planning to ensure there are adequate resources to do the job. Like any other hazard; if fatigue is a concern for you report the issue to your Supervisor/Manager, and/or host organisation and on-hire/contracting firm.

Machinery and Equipment

You might think that risks from machinery only arise in blue collar work, but that’s not true. A variety of machinery and equipment is used in the retail industry including: Guards are often attached to mechanical equipment to protect you from moving parts. You must make sure you leave the guards in place, and that they are replaced by an authorised person if they have been removed for cleaning or maintenance. Machinery must be locked out and isolated during cleaning and maintenance to prevent them being turned on. Remember to follow safe working instructions if they are displayed and if they are not, ask for them. You should also review any warning stickers or posters and check that relevant machinery is firmly fixed to work benches. You should not operate any equipment that is not supported by a safe operating procedure and adequate training.

Sharp Equipment and Tools

Retail work often involves the preparation of products for sale. Therefore, you may be required to use sharp knives, scissors, tools and other equipment. Examples include carton trimmers to cut open cardboard cartons, knives, slicers and mincers for food preparation, as well as trimmers and saws to cut materials to length in places like hardware stores. Cuts and lacerations to hands, fingers and legs are common injuries for workers who frequently open boxes and cut plastic strapping with exposed blades, such as non-retractable utility knives, kitchen knives and scissors. These injuries happen when fingers and hands are in the way when a blade slips or if an open blade is handled unexpectedly. When a blade slips over the edge of the packaging it can strike and cause injury to the leg. A simple control to avoid hand, finger and leg injuries when opening boxes and other similar tasks is to use knives with recessed blades; they prevent the blade coming into contact with body parts. Your workplace may not have these alternatives, however there is nothing stopping you requesting your manager or supervisor to change the types of knives used in the workplace. Some other risk control considerations when using cutting tools and equipment include: Always ask your supervisor or manager for training in the use of sharp tools and equipment if you haven’t been provided with it.

Electrical Hazards

A lot of the machinery and equipment you use in the retail industry is operated by electricity. Again, make sure you only use such equipment following the provision of specific training. You must make sure all electrical machinery and equipment is kept in good working order, electrical plugs and switches are not damaged, cords are not split or frayed, and are tested and checked regularly for damage. Make sure you follow instructions for using electrical equipment. Common electrical safety hazards that should be looked out for and reported to management include:

Remember these basic principles: Remain calm and respectful Use a low, calm tone of voice Listen - don’t intervene too quickly and allow the person a to blow off steam Acknowledge the person’s feelings without diagnosis, encouragement or criticism Paraphrase and summarize what the person is saying by picking out the key points and repeating them out loud. Don’t debate the facts while the person is still angry, and When the person is sufficiently calm it is then appropriate to ask for details of and clarify the complaint or concern. Once you’ve handled the situation, let the appropriate supervisor or employer representative know that they need to address it. But do it politely and be constructive.

Reducing Incidents

There are some basic tips that are good to remember in retail work to reduce the incidence of customer aggression and anger. Ensure that you are aware of the typical security threats in your retail work environment. Your workplace should provide you with the working environment emergency procedures. You should be aware of any working alone procedures; duress alarms; emergency contact numbers and other means to manage security threat situations.

topics.body:
Although you may work in metropolitan or suburban locations, you may be alone.

Cash Handling

In a workplace where cash is handled, you are more likely to face the threat of robbery or attack. To reduce the risk of injury or harm, you should be advised of cash handling procedures which should include:

Mental Health at Work

Did you know that at any one time 1 in 6 working age people will be living with a mental illness? Mental illness is now showcasing as a major contributor to occupational disease and injury statistics in Australia. Common risks to mental health in the workplace include: job stress, bullying and harassment, and workplace trauma. All workers have a right to a work environment that is physical and mentally healthy. Basically, your rights include working conditions that do not cause a mental health condition or aggravate any existing mental health condition. Each workplace approaches mental health in different ways. Your workplace may provide a range of health and wellbeing initiatives and programs, and may include: provision of information, resources and training to create mental health awareness; smarter work design; introducing flexible working hours and creating opportunities for workers to get involved in decision-making processes; stress management and resilience training mentoring and coaching introduction of physical activities in the workplace early intervention programs such as employee assistance program and peer support These initiatives and programs are aimed at cultivating a mentally healthy workplace. As a worker, you also have a part to play. You have duties under the legislation as well when it comes to mental health at work. Looking after you mental health is just as important as looking after your physical health, and as such you must take reasonable care for the mental health of yourself. The way you treat your colleagues and work as a team shapes workplace attitudes and the overall working environment. There are 10 ways in which you can contribute to a mentally healthy workplace: talk openly about mental health at work Share your own personal experience of a mental health condition (if you feel comfortable doing so) Encourage open communication when problems arise and help to find solutions. Respect other people and celebrate difference. Be open to learning about mental health conditions and other people’s experiences. Respect the privacy of others. Be a positive role model - be genuine in your actions and promote the kind of culture that inspires people to do their best. Speak up if you see instances of bullying, harassment or discrimination. Cooperate with workplace policies and procedures, and support initiatives aimed at improving mental health in the workplace. Understand how your workplace can support you and how you can access help if you need it.

In finishing up I want to remind you that it’s critical that you take a proactive approach to workplace safety. Remember the following essentials when performing retail work.
