modules.title: Hospitality Worker Safety
modules.description: This module is appropriate for any hospitality worker, including bar, kitchen and cafe staff, chef, front of house staff, and events workers. The following topics are explored in this module:

topics.title: Welcome
topics.body: Welcome to your work safety induction. Before you get started, there are a few things we need to share with you: This module will take about 30 minutes to complete, not including the assessment You can progress at your own pace using the 'NEXT' and 'BACK' buttons. This module includes audio. If you don't have time to complete all the module in one sitting, the next time you log in you will automatically be presented with the last step you were on. Once you have completed the module: An email will be sent to the requesting organisation. An email will be sent to you for your records. All current modules will be displayed in your online profile.

topics.title: Once you’ve completed this module, you should have a better understanding of the following: the most common hazards and risks in a hospitality working environment; what you can do to prevent these ris
topics.body:
Knives and Knife Safety

A knife is a valuable kitchen tool however it can cause serious injury - depending on your skill and what you know about knife safety. There are some basic safety tips and hints about using a knife properly. Don’t think that if the knife is blunt, it won’t cut you!! An often-unknown fact is that cuts from blunt knives take longer to heal and are generally more serious than cuts from a sharp knife. Case study: What can go wrong? While trying to open a 25 kilo bag of potatoes, the chef sliced the corner of the bag using a 12-inch fish filleting knife. With the knife still in his right hand pointing upwards, he then attempted to move the bag. The cut section of bag gave way causing the knife to be thrust upwards into his face, causing a severe laceration. This is an actual reported incident that shows what can happen when trying to carry a bag whilst still holding a knife. Some other useful tips: Do not use a knife for any other purpose other than cutting. Treat all knife cuts immediately. When carrying a knife, carry it by the handle with the knife pointing down alongside your body. Do not leave a knife on the bench with the blade cutting edge facing up If passing a knife to someone, pass it handle first - Do not throw.

General Food Safety

If you are going to be working with or around food on a more permanent basis then you may need to have a Food Handlers certificate. If you don’t have one or you have been asked to work in the kitchen for only a couple of hours, here are some basic things to remember about food safety:

topics.title: Manual Tasks
topics.body:
Manual tasks are high risk in hospitality, as most of the work involves some kind of bending, lifting or twisting and other activities involving the exertion of force. Now before we start, I just wanted to let you know that manual tasks are not only about lifting. Any time that you need to use force to move, lift, push, pull, hold or carry an object is a manual task. So you can see from that definition that a lot of tasks in hospitality are manual task related.

Manual Tasks (cont.)

Manual task related injuries account for approximately half of the total lost time injuries in the cafe and restaurant industry. Industry injury data shows that kitchen hands, cooks, waiters and chefs across all age categories sustain the highest number of injuries. Most of the injuries occur when lifting, handling or reaching and most commonly result in sprains and strains of muscles and joints. Some examples of where manual task hazards can arise in hospitality include: Repetitively reaching for glasses or bottles above shoulder height; Bending or balancing whilst serving; Lifting cases and cartons of food, beverages and other goods; Taking rubbish out Standing or sitting at a register collecting money; Unloading and storing stock items; Moving heavy or awkward furniture or equipment; Cleaning or washing cooking equipment, crockery, cutlery or glasses. Carrying piles of plates Lifting baskets of dirty dishes Stretching across tables or reaching over the counter Case study: What can go wrong? A new waiter was copying more experienced waiters and carrying the same amount of dirty plates when clearing tables. The waiter was not carrying the dirty plates correctly as he thought his way was quicker. He was able to keep up with them for the first part of the dinner service, but as the night wore on he became fatigued. Just before he finished his shift, whilst putting platters in the storeroom, he strained a muscle in his lower back from over reaching. This is an actual reported incident that shows what can happen when trying to carry or lift things incorrectly.

topics.title: Safe Lifting Techniques
topics.body: It is vital that when you are in a workplace where you are constantly handling products and moving equipment, stock, foodstuffs and furniture, that you lift things safely. The first rule that we have is that if there is a trolley available or another form of mechanical aid then use them, they don’t break down as easily!! If there aren’t any trolleys available make sure you adhere to the following:

topics.title: Reduce Manual Task Risks
topics.body: Other things you can do to reduce manual task risks in hospitality work, is to avoid the need for bending and twisting movements or the exertion of physical force, especially if it’s repetitive or regular. In some cases it may require an automated process to overcome the risk, and this is something else you should remember. Don’t think everything has to be done manually, there’s often a less risky and quicker way of doing a job by using specialised equipment.

topics.title: Tips to Reduce Manual Task Risks
topics.body: Some other tips for reducing manual task risks are: When carrying, break loads into smaller quantities. Think about carrying smaller trays of glasses and a smaller stack of plates or use smaller baskets for cleaning tables. If you need to carry soiled linen i.e. tablecloths then try and carry small amounts as they are heavy and awkward to hold. Always push a trolley - do not pull. This reduces the risk of injuring yourself and you can see where you are going. Make sure stock and other items that are regularly used are not stored above shoulder height or below mid-thigh level. All common items should be stored between hip and chest height. Avoid putting heavy objects on the floor or up high where they have to be lifted or lowered Use a work table that is right for your height where possible and try to put objects at waist height to reduce bending Arrange for deliveries to be unloaded directly to where they are needed. Make sure you can always see where you are going do not carry a load in such a way that it blocks your vision. Do not lift anything beyond your capability - ask for help if necessary. When doing tasks such as mopping, chopping, painting, grinding, sweeping and vacuuming, change your hands, maintain good posture and break up repetitive tasks. Keep floors, loading dock areas, passages and aisle ways clear and free of obstacles at all times. Do not jump from one level to another (for example from a ramp to the ground). Advise your Supervisor/Manager immediately if you injure yourself or see a potential hazard. Finally, remember you can ask for training in correct manual handling techniques, you’re entitled to be trained.

topics.title: First Aid
topics.body:
If you are injured at work you may need first aid. Like emergency procedures, some places you work will do it very well while others may not. Below are some points to be mindful of about first aid at the workplace: Know where the first aid kit is for your work site. Know the procedure for first aid. Know who the first aid warden is at the workplace. If you are not sure, ASK!!

Electrical Hazards

Exposure to electrical hazards is something that must be taken very seriously. You must make sure all electrical machinery and equipment is kept in good working order, electrical plugs and switches are not damaged, cords are not split or frayed, and are tested and checked regularly for damage. And remember, if you receive any sort of electric shock from a cord or appliance then turn it off at the switch and notify your Manager or Supervisor. You must also follow instructions for using electrical equipment. Common electrical safety hazards that should be looked out for and reported to management include: This is an actual reported incident that shows what can happen when we mistreat electrical appliances and don’t follow some simple rules.

topics.title: General Tips for using Electrical Equipment
topics.body: As a general rule you should always: Ask qualified people about the most appropriate electrical equipment for the task and don’t guess or try and use your initiative when you simply don’t know; If you find a piece of damaged or faulty equipment tag it as “Out of Service” and immediately notify your supervisor and work mates; and Never attempt to repair the damaged or faulty equipment yourself.

topics.title: Hazardous Chemicals
topics.body: Many hospitality environments require workers to work with or near hazardous chemicals such as cleaning agents. Hazardous chemicals are substances that can harm the health of people using them and they come in liquid, solid and gas form. If these chemicals are inhaled, absorbed through the skin or swallowed you may suffer immediate or long-term effects to your health. It’s vitally important that hazardous chemicals are used and stored in the correct manner. The best way of determining correct use and storage is to obtain a copy of a document called a safety data sheet or what is generically called an SDS. The other piece of equipment you will need to familiarise yourself with is PPE. PPE stands for Personal Protective Equipment and this includes things such as safety glasses, gloves, masks, aprons etc. These are some of the items that must be worn when doing certain tasks such as using chemicals. You will find all of this information on the SDS so familiarise yourself with it before commencing work. Listed below are some simple rules that you need to apply when using chemicals at work:

topics.title: The Safety Data Sheet (SDS)
topics.body: An SDS should be stored in a specially designated location within the workplace. You should be advised of their location prior to using any chemicals. If you can’t find the SDS then ask your Supervisor or Manager.

topics.title: Burns and Scalds
topics.body: A lot of hospitality work involves the preparation and service of hot food and drinks, so the risk of burns and scalds is very high, so you need to take care when dealing with hot food and equipment. Think about the following risk control measures: Wear personal protective equipment where possible including such things as heat resistant gloves; Use a waiter’s cloth to protect your arms while carrying hot plates; Make sure you demand training in the service of food where needed; and Cover equipment containing hot fat or fluids when they’re not being used. There are many systems that should be in place to prevent burns and scalds so in addition to these risk control measures ask your Supervisor whether risk assessments have been completed in your work area.

topics.title: Storage Area Safety
topics.body: Sometimes you might be asked to work in a storage area or loading dock in hospitality work. These areas are extremely dangerous and you shouldn’t be in them unless you’ve been trained and inducted. Some specific storage area safety principles should be remembered if required to work in such areas:

topics.title: Slips and Trips
topics.body: One of the most common causes of injury within the hospitality industry is when a worker or customer slips or trips. There are plenty of causes:

topics.title: Biological Waste and Sharps
topics.body: An unfortunate side of working in the hospitality industry is that you may be exposed to biological waste hazards such as blood, bodily fluids and vomit. You may also be exposed to objects that can pierce or penetrate the skin. We call these ‘sharps’, and they include broken glass and syringes. It is critical that you understand that biological waste and sharps present a very real risk to your health and safety and that you shouldn’t be required to pick or clean them up unless you have been fully trained and provided with the appropriate protective equipment to do it safely. As a general rule, remember the following if you are exposed to biological waste and sharps in the workplace: The organisation with control of the workplace should have systems in place for the safe removal of biological waste and sharps; There should be a register of hot spots where sharps and biological waste are regularly found, such as toilets, where trained professionals deal with such waste; There should be dedicated containers for sharps in workplaces where they are commonly used; and Don’t manually compress garbage bags or other containers where sharps can puncture the skin. Remember, cleaning of biological waste and sharps requires specialist knowledge and equipment and it is not just part of any hospitality job so don’t do it if you’re not confident or know how to do it safely.

topics.title: Outdoor Work
topics.body: If you are working outdoors you should be provided with equipment to protect yourself from UV radiation, such as broad-brim hats, sunglasses and clothing with the appropriate UPF (UV Protection factor). If you are working outdoors and haven’t been provided with sunscreen as a minimum, then you need to ask your Supervisor/Manager. Some things that we want you to remember when working outdoors, particularly in the sun: Make sure you wear a broad brimmed hat and wear sunglasses if you are spending long periods outside. Wear 30 + sunscreen. Put it on 15 minutes before you go out in the sun and put it on regularly (see the label for instructions) Have regular drinks of cool water - do not wait until you are thirsty. If you can, try to plan your day so that you spend as little time in the sun as you can. Some things that we want you to remember when working outdoors, particularly if it’s cold: Wear the correct uniform, as it may be designed to protect you from cold winds. Ask your Supervisor/Manager if they have a wind proof or waterproof jacket. If possible, wear layers of clothing so that if it warms up during the day you can always take them off. If you get wet then try and change your clothes as quickly as possible. If you know you are going to be working outside and the weather forecast is for rain then pack an extra pair of socks. At least you may be able to change into these later in the day and keep your feet warm.

topics.title: Operating equipment
topics.body: There is some equipment that cannot be operated unless you have a specific licence but for the majority of the equipment that you will operate, a licence is not necessary. Here are some basic rules about operating equipment: If you don’t know how to use the equipment - ask for instruction or training. Don’t operate equipment that you haven’t been shown how to use. Never touch moving parts of machinery or equipment. Report damaged equipment to your Supervisor or Manager immediately. Don’t try and fix it yourself.

topics.title: Stress
topics.body: Did you know workplace stress is the second most common cause of workplace compensation claims in Australia after manual handling? Stress claims cost businesses $10.11 billion p.a. due to loss of productivity and absenteeism. This figure is likely to be under-represented however as it doesn’t include unsuccessful claims and those who do not make a formal claim. So what does stress actually mean? The World Health Organisation defines stress as “the reaction people may have when presented with demands and pressures that are not matched to their knowledge and abilities and which challenge their ability to cope”. Stress can occur in a wide range of situations, is complex and typically has multiple causes. Many jobs involve negative factors that put unwanted pressure (stress) on the worker, leading to adverse consequences. Stress is not a disease or injury in itself, but can lead to mental and physical ill health, and can also be a factor in workplace incidents.

topics.title: What Causes Workplace Stress
topics.body:
Negative Stress

So, how is negative stress identified in the workplace? There are many different potential work-related stress hazards and risks in the workplace. You should be aware of systematic processes that the organisation undertakes to identify these hazards and risks. These processes should involve consultation with the workforce including you as a worker. Risks to psychological health in the workplace can largely be categorised as those relating to the social and physical work environment, the way that work is organised (system of work) and the way that work is managed. Some aspects of the social and physical environment that have the potential to cause harm are: role in the organisation career development, status and pay conflicting home/work demands physical work environment and equipment

topics.title: Stress and Systems of Work
topics.body: Issues relating to the way that work is organised (system of work) can include: the content and demands of the work the workload and pace of the work work schedules and working hours the extent of participation and control that people have over the work The way that work is managed can have harmful effects relating to: inadequate or unsupportive supervision lack of suitable information, instruction and training to enable employees to do their work

topics.title: Identifying & Managing Stress
topics.body: As a worker your employer owes you a duty of care. This duty of care extends to ensuring that your health and safety is not at risk; the meaning of health includes ‘psychological health’. Duty holders should be taking reasonable steps to eliminate or reduce the risk of negative stress. If you are a contractor, the on-hire/contracting firm can play a significant role in identifying and managing negative stress. Expect that your on-hire/contracting firm does the following: provides you with key job information (tasks, safety aspects, working hours including overtime, expected break times, remote work or working in isolation, reporting structure) maintains regular contact with you and offers opportunities to report any health and safety concerns associated with the contract assignment. For the Host, expect systems to manage the following areas: work environment systems of work work tasks If you feel you are exposed to negative stressors – report it to your supervisor/manager and (if appropriate) your on hire/contracting firm!

topics.title: Tips for dealing with Workplace Stress
topics.body:
You need to take some responsibility for identifying and managing stress, so here are some key points to consider:

Summary

In finishing up I want to remind you that it’s critical that you take a proactive approach to workplace safety. When you wait for others to control risks in the workplace that’s when accidents occur. Remember the following essentials when performing hospitality work: Hospitality environments are often unsafe; Complacency in hospitality environments contributes to injury and illness Don’t wait for somebody else to fix the problem, be proactive; and Don’t do work you haven’t been trained to do safely.

modules.title: Forklift Safety Operation
modules.description: This module has been developed to remind individuals of some of the most important elements of safe forklift operations. It does not replace formal training to gain a forklift licence. This module includes:

topics.title: Welcome
topics.body:
Welcome to your work safety induction. Before you get started, there are a few things we need to share with you: This module will take about 30 minutes to complete, not including the assessment You can progress at your own pace using the 'NEXT' and 'BACK' buttons. This module includes audio. If you don't have time to complete all the module in one sitting, the next time you log in you will automatically be presented with the last step you were on. Once you have completed the module: An email will be sent to the requesting organisation. An email will be sent to you for your records. All current modules will be displayed in your online profile.

Introduction Forklift safety is a serious safety concern because of the interaction of forklifts, other vehicles and pedestrians in the workplace. This module will focus on forklift hazards and precautionary measures to ensure the safe operation of forklifts. Before we get started, we need to familiarise you with some terms that will be used across this module: Person or Persons Conducting a Business or Undertaking (PCBU) You may or may not be familiar with the term Persons Conducting a Business or Undertaking (PCBU). This term refers to a businesses and not-for-profit organisations. An individual can also be a PCBU, but only if they are a sole trader. Basically, a PCBU replaces the term ‘employer’; it is the company or individual who has management, control and influence over work tasks and activities. There may be more than one PCBU in your workplace, for example, if you are an on-hire worker, the PCBUs are the on-hire firm and the host company. For the ease of reading, we will refer to a PCBU as an ‘Employer’ throughout this module. Workers The term worker refers to any person engaged by the PCBU to undertake work. This includes employees, contractors and subcontractors, apprentices, persons gaining work experience, on-hire workers, outworkers and volunteers. For the purposes of inclusion, we will refer to all persons engaged by the PCBU as ‘workers’.

Duties in the Workplace

Health and safety regimes are genuinely aimed at providing workers and others in the workplace with a work environment that is safe and without risk to health. As such, everyone in the workplace has a health and safety responsibility and duty of care. When it comes to forklift safety, employers, designers, suppliers and workers all have duties. Let’s firstly explore the duties for employers and workers. Employers – PCBUs/employers have a primary duty to eliminate or minimise the risks associated with forklift operation. They need to ensure the provision and maintenance of safe plant, including forklifts, as well as ensuring the safe use, handling, storage and transport of forklifts. (NOTE: Please click on the video link AFTER you have finished reading the content on this page. The video will open in a seperate window.) The following video – Forklifts hitting pedestrians video safety alert provides an insight into some simple controls that employers can implement to manage the risks associated with forklift operation. You may find a combination of these risk control measures at your workplace. Workers – workers have a duty to take reasonable care for their own health and safety, and co-operate with reasonable policies and procedures that the employer has in place regarding forklift safety. Workers have a duty to not adversely affect other people’s health and safety. Basically: If you are operating a forklift, you must hold a high-risk work licence If your workplace has safe work procedures regarding forklift safety, you should follow these Do not carry out any unsafe acts when operating the forklift that may put yours and others safety at risk

topics.title: Training & Supervision
topics.body: The law takes forklift operation seriously and as such any person that operates a forklift requires a high-risk work forklift licence or must be under the direct supervision of a person with a high-risk work forklift licence who has suitable workplace experience. Below is a table that identifies the types of forklift trucks and whether an operator licence is required. These licence requirements are applicable for all States and Territories in Australia. For operation of a forklift in New Zealand, a forklift licence consists of two parts, the F endorsement and the OSH certificate. (OSH is a term that is used in the industry to refer to a division of the Department of Labour). The OSH certificate entitles you to drive a forklift. The F endorsement entitles you to drive a forklift where there may be public or on public roads. The OSH certificate expires every 3 years, while the F endorsement does not expire. In addition to a high risk work forklift licence, it is expected that as a forklift operator, you will receive a workplace specific induction and training in safe forklift operation, including the site specific traffic management plan. The Risks Forklifts are one of the most dangerous pieces of equipment found in workplaces. A medium-sized forklift weighs as much as a dump truck – and can cause as much damage and injury. Forklift instability can result in the forklift overturning which can result in serious injury and even fatality. It is important to be aware of the hazards and risks associated with forklifts.

topics.title: Forklift Hazards
topics.body:
Forklift Fundamentals

Before any work commences with a forklift, including pre-start checks, operators should follow safe work practices and don their personal protective equipment. PPE required at your workplace for operation in and around forklifts may include: Pre-start forklift checks are a crucial forklift safety fundamental.

Pre-Start Checks

Operation Fundamentals

In addition to the pre-start checks, there are operation fundamentals that must always be considered and adopted by the forklift operator; these include:

topics.title: Operation Fundamentals Cont’d
topics.body: Forklift fundamentals extend to parking and shut down of the forklift. The first fundamental for parking and shutdown is to remove the ignition key or lock off the start control when the forklift is unattended; this is to stop unauthorized use.

topics.title: Parking
topics.body:
The Risks

Forklift Instability Forklifts have a compact design. They are designed this way so they can get in, out and around tight spaces. Because of their compact nature, forklifts are a lot less stable than other vehicles or mobile plant. It might seem unlikely, but an unstable forklift can quite easily roll over or tip. In fact, around one in six overturned forklifts result in operator death. Some of the causes of forklift tips or rolls include: Cornering too fast or turning too sharply Braking too quickly while carrying a load Driving across inclines or uneven ground Driving with raised forks, both with or without a load Colliding with another vehicle Hitting low doors or beams Carrying an unbalanced load We welcome you to take a look at this video on Forklift safety at work. This video reinforces some of the key safety rules when operating a forklift.

topics.title: Managing Forklift
topics.body:
Managing Forklift Instability Those in control of the workplace have a duty to provide a safe working environment. An important part of this is making sure you are properly trained in all aspects of your role. As a forklift operator you must be instructed on safe forklift practice, which includes being shown how to correctly operate and maintain the forklift, as well as how to follow traffic management procedures. You have a role to play in ensuring forklift safety in the workplace. If you are asked to operate a forklift and haven’t received the training, don’t do it! Too many incidents occur because the person operating the machinery didn’t feel comfortable using it and had not received adequate training and supervision. By operating a forklift when it is not safe to do so, you are not only placing yourself at serious risk, but also the safety of others in the workplace. If you are involved in an incident where a forklift has overturned or tipped, the safest place for you to be is in the cabin with a seatbelt on. Most of the serious injuries or deaths that occur in an unstable forklift incident happen when the operator jumps from the cabin and is crushed. It’s also a good idea to lean in the opposite direction to the overturn. Those in management and control of the workplace can take various steps in reducing the risk of forklift instability. If there are any concerns about forklift safety at your workplace, you should speak up. Minimising the chance of a forklift overturning is important for everybody in the workplace and should be a priority for management and workers.

Forklift Speed and Breaking Distance

In the case of an emergency, how fast a forklift will be able to stop depends on a number of things. These include the weight of the load it’s carrying, how fast it is going, and the surface it’s traveling on. Research shows that one of the main dangers of breaking suddenly while carrying a load is that the load might fall from the forks, or the forklift might tip or roll over. It stands to reason that forklift breaking distances must be considered when planning for, and managing forklift travel paths. Did you know that even if traveling at walking pace it still takes a forklift about three metres to stop? And at a speed of 12 km/h a forklift needs about eight metres to stop safely. That’s a pretty big distance to cover under braking conditions. Reducing the Risks Associated with Forklift Speed Too many workplaces rely on the operator to stop the forklift using nothing more than his or her own judgment. But judgment is something that comes with experience, and even experienced people sometimes make mistakes. Good ways of reducing the risks associated with forklift speed are to: Determine and enforce forklift speed limits based on a proper risk assessment, taking into account stability under brakes, and stopping distance Display speed limits and signs in clear view of operators and those within the work environment Construct and clearly mark pedestrian walkways, roadways and forklift operating areas that provide effective traffic separation based on speed limits and stopping distances Ensure speed limiting devices are fitted to forklifts

topics.title: Loads and Load Handling
topics.body: Like forklifts themselves, loads can be heavy. It’s not just the weight of the load that needs to be considered; shape, size and composition are important factors as well. This is why it’s important to be familiar with a load before carrying it. The right forklift design for the load to be lifted or suspended is a must! Any attachments used to lift the load need to be within safe working limits of the forklift. The forklift you operate should have the manufacturer’s data plate and load chart attached in clear view. The load chart should clearly identify the load capacity in kilograms, which is the maximum weight the forklift can carry at certain load centre distance (mm) and at maximum lift height (metres) with vertical mast. It is important to note that the lifting capacity of a forklift should be reduced by a safety factor of at least 20% when handling bulk bags such as intermediate bulk containers.

topics.title: Loads and Load Handling Cont’d
topics.body: There is also the risk of falling loads. Falling loads are among the biggest hazards when it comes to forklift safety. Each time you carry a load you need to follow correct safety procedure to avoid the risks of a load falling on pedestrians or you, the operator. If you are in control of a suspended load, then there are key control measures that need to be put in place to ensure the safety of yourself and others in the workplace. Do not perform dragging or off-vertical lifts with a suspended load Ensure the load is secured across both fork arms and is secured with an suitable attachment Ensure the load remains within the rated capacity of the forklift Keep the load as low as possible whilst traveling Move slowly and cautiously when the load is raised

topics.title: Attachments
topics.body: Attachments can affect the load rating of a forklift, and as such there are some important factors you need to keep in mind and act on when operating a forklift with an attachment.

topics.title: Work Platforms & Boxes
topics.body: Firstly, it’s obvious that it is clearly not safe to use a forklift pallets or bare fork arms to raise individuals to a position of height – the consequences are significant. If someone needs to be raised, there are particular types of machinery, such as scissor lifts or cherry pickers that can do the job in a far safer way than a forklift. The primary design of a forklift is for lifting and manoeuvring loads, not people. There are however some industrial lift trucks that are designed to lift people such as the ‘order picking industrial lift truck’. A separate work platform or work box that is fitted to a forklift can be used to lift people under strict conditions and should only be used for occasional tasks. A trial lift, without the person in the box should take place as a practice run to ensure all safety measures are in place including checking for overhead obstructions and power lines. The person(s) working in the work box: Needs to be securely attached Stay within the workbox Where there is a risk of falling, wear a safety harness Can exit the workbox in a safe manner, including where the industrial lift truck fails in its normal operation

topics.title: Ventilation
topics.body: Poor Ventilation Resulting in Exposure to Harmful Gas Emissions While electrically powered forklifts are becoming more common, many forklifts are still powered by combustion engines which use petrol, diesel or LPG. These release harmful gasses such as carbon monoxide, a colorless, odorless gas that can cause serious health effects. To avoid harmful exposure, workplaces using forklifts powered by combustion engines must have appropriate airflow. Allowing this type of forklift to operate in closed spaces is far too dangerous because exposure to gases not only impairs your judgment and reflexes but can also cause dizziness and fatigue – this is not my idea of a safe workplace. So, if your workplace does not use electric forklifts, make sure the work area is really well ventilated and report any concerns immediately to your supervisor.

topics.title: Slips, Trips and Falls While Getting on or Off Forklifts
topics.body:
It’s a fact that one third of all forklift injuries occur when an operator is getting on or off a forklift. Observing simple safety practice helps reduce the risk of injury. These include: Checking that the park brake is on when getting off the forklift, and that the forks are lowered and the controls in neutral before alighting Not jumping from the forklift Ensuring each forklift has steps that give a good footing, anti-slip surfaces and grab-rails Minimising the need to get on and off forklifts by re-working work practices Making sure forklift operating and parking areas are well lit and clear of obstructions Even things such as the layout of foot pedals, the steering wheel position and the cabin floor surface can help to reduce slips, trips and falls so familiarise yourself with the design of the forklift.

Sprains and Strains While Operating a Forklift

Awkward postures such as looking behind whilst driving in reverse and sitting in the forklift for long periods can contribute to muscle related injuries. In addition, back strains can be caused by driving on uneven surfaces. If the seat of a forklift is in poor condition, driving over bumps on a repetitive basis may result in back stress. Good ways to manage the risks associated with sprains and strains are: Ensuring the operator’s seat and cabin are in good condition Using vision aids such as closed-circuit video systems which reduce neck twisting Maintaining level ground surfaces in the forklift operating area Using forklifts that are ergonomically designed to reduce the effort required to operate controls, steer and break

topics.title: Ramps & Loading Docks
topics.body: If ramps or loading docks are a part of your forklift operation duties, there are a number of important risk control measures: Check the ramps are wide enough and provide enough clearance for the forklift to safely operate Ensure the mast is tilted back enough to support the load and reduce the risk of it moving from the fork arms When travelling up or down a slope, the load should be placed on the uphill side Ensure the fork arms are on the downhill side when you are travelling without a load (this is the opposite to the above) If you are driving the load into another vehicle, ensure that checks are made regarding the stability of the floor surface you are planning to drive the forklift onto. It should be able to safely hold the forklift and the load.

topics.title: Working Near Electrical Lines
topics.body:
Planning lifts and checking overhead is crucial in preventing contact with electrical lines. Exposure to electrical lines carries heavy consequences. Contact with energised overhead or underground electrical lines can be fatal and as such it is important to ensure, that when you are operating a forklift, no part of yourself, any other person or the forklift you are operating comes within an unsafe distance of an overhead or underground electric line.

Fuel Handling and Storage

Storage and handling of liquid fuel should be carried out in accordance with the relevant standards for storage and use of flammable and combustible liquids. LPG engine powered forklifts should be used and parked in well-ventilated areas and a safe distance from any source of heat and iginition. Only suitably trained people should remove empty LPG cylinders from forklifts and install full LPG cylinders. When the forklift is not in operation, the LPG cylinder valve should be turned off.

Battery Charging & Changing

From time to time, a forklift battery may need to be charged or changed. The activity of forklift battery charging and changing should only be carried out by those who have received adequate training and instruction. For those that have received the relevant training, when charging or changing the battery, should wear the required personal protective equipment (PPE). Before the battery is charged, the operator must ensure that the forklift is parked with the handbrake on and check the vent caps in the batteries are functioning correctly and stay in place during charging to prevent electrolyte spraying. There is a risk of explosive hydrogen gas generating during the charging process, therefore it is important to remember to allow the gases to escape. This can be done by ensuring the cover over the battery is held open during charging.

topics.title: Out of Service
topics.body: Your workplace should have a procedure for plant and equipment that is ‘out-of-service’ and it is crucial that you follow your workplace’s procedure if you find a fault in the forklift that you are operating. For forklifts that have a fault and are unsafe to operate you should: Report the fault to your supervisor Follow your workplace’s out-of-service procedure for identification and isolation of the forklift The forklift should remain out-of-service until it has been repaired and has returned to a safe state. For damaged forklifts, a competent person should undertake an assessment and prepare a report on the status and safety of the forklift. The forklift should not be operated until the assessment and report have been considered by management, and the forklift deemed safe to return to normal operation.

topics.title: Forklift Maintenance and Operator Checklist
topics.body: Forklift maintenance plays an important role in preventing breakdowns and other mechanical failures. Causes of faults affecting the safe operation of forklifts include faulty brakes, poor tyre and seat condition, and faulty warning lights or operator controls. Proper forklift inspection, using an operator checklist helps reduce the chance of operating a forklift that is unsafe. Using an operator checklist, you should assess the operating condition of the forklift, and check things such things as tyres, fluids, seating, warning devices, breaks and operator controls. Work health and safety law guides suggest the following for operator forklift checks: If any items on the checklist do not meet the required safety standard, do not operate the forklift. You must tell your Supervisor who should ensure that the forklift is not operated again until it is safe. Do not take chances. Safety mechanisms such as warning lights are attached to your forklift for a reason and do prevent injuries and fatalities. So, make sure they are in good working order before you start.

topics.title: Pedestrians and Traffic Management Planning
topics.body: A traffic management plan safely separates or defines pedestrian areas from mobile plant areas. The aim is to reduce or remove the chance of mobile plant and people colliding. In order to do this, the work environment needs to undergo a risk assessment, and the best people to assess the risks are those who work in the environment each day. This includes your workmates, Supervisor, Health and Safety Representatives, as well as forklift or other mobile plant operators. Once these risks have been identified, the parties need to set about developing control measures to reduce or remove the risks altogether. A traffic management plan needs to be readily accessible so that all those at the workplace, including visitors, are aware of how to move around the work environment safely. Below are some examples of traffic management controls: Clearly define forklift and pedestrian areas, using signage to exclude pedestrian travel in forklift zones Put in place barriers to separate and protect marked pedestrian walkways and forklift zones Use proximity devices to trigger signals and boom gates, and ensure forklift warning devices and flashing lights are functioning at all times Ensure pedestrians wear high visibility clothing and/or reflective vests Provide training on forklift traffic safety to anyone who enters the site, be they employees or visitors Ensure forklift operators stop work if pedestrians enter a pedestrian exclusion zone Pedestrians generally think that forklift operators can see them as well as they can see the operator, but unfortunately that isn’t always the case.

topics.title: Summary
topics.body: In finishing up I want to remind you that it’s critical that you take a proactive approach to workplace safety. This induction module has helped you identify risks and hazards involved with operating a forklift. It has also provided tips for preventing or minimising these risks. Your ticket, this training and site induction should now enable you and your workmates operate in a safer environment.

topics.title: Introduction The workforce is highly diverse. It consists of people from different racial or ethnic backgrounds, with various political and religious beliefs, sexual orientation and physical abilities
topics.body:
Discrimination and the Law

We just mentioned some of the personal characteristics upon which people, or groups of people, can be discriminated against at work. Some examples of how people might be treated unfairly based on their personal characteristics include: Being unfairly singled out or having less opportunity because you are different in some way often amounts to discrimination, and this is unacceptable and often unlawful. Later we’ll talk about what you should do if you feel you are being discriminated against.

Discrimination Isn’t Always What You Think

It can be unlawful discrimination if you assume a person has a particular characteristic or attribute, and you discriminate against them on the basis of such an assumption when, in fact, they actually don’t have such characteristics or attributes. For example, assuming somebody has a certain sexual orientation, and treating them differently based on this belief or assumption will still constitute a breach of discrimination law. It’s important to remember that it can also be unlawful discrimination if you treat somebody unfairly because they are friends with somebody else who has different personal characteristics. An example would be treating somebody unfairly because they are friends with somebody at work who is Muslim. Remember that discrimination doesn’t have to be intentional. For example, you can actually be in breach of the law if you tell a religious joke that offends somebody in the workplace when you don’t even know they respect that religion.

topics.title: Sexual Harassment
topics.body: Just like discrimination, you’ve probably heard of sexual harassment. Sexual harassment is any unwelcome behaviour of a sexual nature that can make a person feel humiliated, intimidated or offended. Sexual harassment may include but is not limited to: Sexual harassment can be intentional or unintentional and is not sexual interaction, flirtation, attraction or friendship which is invited, mutual, or consensual.

topics.title: Sexual Harassment and the Law
topics.body: Everyone has the right to be safe and free from harassment while at work. Behaviour that is sexually offensive to somebody else in the workplace is against the law, and all workplaces and employees are responsible for keeping the work environment free from inappropriate sexual conduct. A single incident may amount to sexual harassment depending on the circumstances. For example, a single remark may be so offensive as to amount to sexual harassment in itself, but an unwanted invitation out may not constitute sexual harassment if it is not repeated. Sexual harassment is unlawful in any work-related context, including conferences, work functions, office parties and business or field trips and includes interactions with clients and customers. Sexual harassment is prohibited under Australian State and Federal legislation as well as International legislation.

topics.title: Workplace Harassment
topics.body:
As in sexual harassment, it can be seen as 'workplace harassment' if you are subjected to repeated behaviour, by a person, including your employer or a colleague or group of colleagues and:

Harassment (Continued)

Workplace harassment can be intentional or unintentional. Examples of the more common types of behaviours that may be regarded as workplace harassment (if the behaviour is repeated or occurs as part of a pattern of behaviour) include: abusing a person loudly, either in private or when others are present; repeated threats of dismissal or other severe punishment for no reason; constant ridicule and being put down; leaving offensive messages on email, telephone or potentially via social media; sabotaging a person's work, for example, deliberately withholding or supplying incorrect information, hiding documents or equipment, and not passing on messages; maliciously excluding and isolating a person from workplace activities; persistent and unjustified criticisms, often about petty, irrelevant or insignificant matters; humiliating a person through gestures, sarcasm, criticism and insults, both in private or in front of customers, Managers or other staff; and spreading gossip or false, malicious rumours about a person with or without an intent to cause the person harm.

topics.title: Victimisation
topics.body: It’s also against the law to threaten or treat people less favourably as a result of them raising or supporting allegations of discrimination, harassment or bullying. It may be considered victimisation if a person has suffered some form of detriment because they have, for example, lodged a complaint of discrimination or sexual harassment, attended a conciliation conference or reasonably asserted their rights, or supported someone else’s rights.

topics.title: How to Respond to Discrimination and Sexual Harassment
topics.body: If you believe you have been discriminated against, sexually or otherwise harassed or victimised in the workplace there are numerous options available to try and have the matter resolved. These include:

topics.title: Bullying
topics.body: Bullying can happen in any workplace and it can have an impact on an individual’s health, both mentally and physically and affect their ability to do their job. Workplace bullying is characterised by persistent and repeated negative behaviour directed towards a worker or group of workers that creates a risk to health and safety. The common features of bullying are: Repeated behaviour Unreasonable behaviour, directed towards a worker/group of workers Behaviour that creates a risk to health and safety

topics.title: Bullying (Continued)
topics.body:
Examples of behaviour, whether intentional or unintentional, that may be considered workplace bullying is if it is repeated, unreasonable and creates a risk to health and safety. This includes but is not limited to:

Impacts of Bullying

Workplace bullying can have significant human impact, and may include:

Your Duty

You have a duty under the work health and safety laws to take reasonable care to ensure your behaviour does not adversely affect the health and safety of others at the workplace. The health and safety of a co-worker doesn’t only relate to their physical wellbeing, it also includes their emotional or mental health. Treating someone in an undermining or unreasonable way negatively impacts upon their health and safety. You also have a duty to comply with any reasonable instruction provided to you and co-operate with any reasonable policies and procedures, such as a workplace bullying policy.

topics.title: The duty of your Employer
topics.body: The business you are working for has a primary duty of care to ensure that the workplace is without risks to workers and other person’s health and safety. You should expect your workplace to have the following systems in place to prevent and respond to bullying: Workplace Bullying Policy Reporting and Response Procedures Training & Information A process to monitor and review control measures

topics.title: Reasonable Management Action
topics.body:
To be clear, ‘Reasonable management action’ is performance management that is undertaken in a reasonable way. Here is a legal example:

Responding to Bullying (Internal Process)

Responding to Bullying (External Process)

In 2013, amendments to the Fair Work Act were made in Australia and empowered the Fair Work Commission to make orders to stop bullying. This legislation took affect from 1 January 2014. topics.title: Welcome
topics.body:
Work Health Safety (WHS) Responsibilities

Employers WHS law places a duty of care on the employer to provide a healthy and safe working environment. The employer must ensure they do whatever they can (in other words, whatever is ‘reasonably practicable’) to ensure that workers and other persons are not put at risk from work carried out as part of their business. Moreover, the employer must ensure that the following are without risks to health and safety: the workplace, including entry and exit and anything arising from the workplace; the fixtures, fittings or plant; the plant, substance or structure. You should receive necessary instruction, supervision and training from both your employer and anybody else responsible for the management and control of your workplace. Not only will you complete this induction, but you should also receive a workplace and company specific induction from your employer prior to commencing work. You should also receive job specific training, instruction and supervision as necessary from a suitably qualified individual. Workers As a ‘worker’, you have a duty of care; this duty is to take reasonable care for your own health and safety, as well as others. You must also co-operate with the employer in compliance with the WHS legislation, this includes following any policy or procedure that has been notified to workers and implemented by the employer to ensure health and safety at the workplace.

topics.title: Consultation
topics.body: If we don’t report hazards, they may not be acted on, and if we don´t give our suggestions to what controls might work well, the hazard may not be adequately managed; therefore consultation is a very important process to the risk management process. It is also a duty of the employer to consult on matters that can directly affect your health and safety. So what is Consultation? Consultation is a 3 step process, it involves: sharing of information; giving workers a reasonable opportunity to express views; and taking those views into account before making decisions on health and safety matters. As a worker your employer owes you a duty to consult with you, ensuring that you have an opportunity to express your views on matters that may directly affect your health and safety.

topics.title: Issue Resolution
topics.body: So what’s the process if you need to raise a health and safety issue? The employer that you are working for may have an agreed issue resolution procedure, therefore you would need to make yourself aware of this procedure and follow the process. Generally, an issue resolution procedure requires the following steps: Report the health and safety issue to your Manager and the health and safety representative (HSR) (if there is one), Discuss the issue with your Manager and HSR, If the discussions do not lead to a resolution, any party can contact the relevant State Health & Safety Authority who will send an inspector to the workplace to assist in resolving the health and safety issue. This request should only be made after reasonable efforts have been made to achieve an effective resolution of the issue.

topics.title: Your Responsibility
topics.body: What are you responsible for as an employee? Take reasonable care to protect your own health and safety, and others potentially affected by your actions at work. Comply with all laws, policies, procedures and safety instructions. Co-operate with your employer on any actions taken to ensure health and safety. This includes: Following workplace health and safety policies and procedures; Using risk control measures provided to you; Attending workplace health and safety training; Reporting hazards and risks in the workplace. Hold licences, permits or qualifications as required. Equipment, including personal protective equipment must be used by you as directed, stored appropriately and kept in good working condition. Report all workplace hazards, mishaps, and incidents, including near misses on the day they occur. Incidents should be reported to your employer and your workplace manager or Supervisor.

topics.title: Starting your new role
topics.body: When starting in your new role you should receive a company induction which introduces you to the workplace and the workplace policies and procedures. Following your company induction you should receive appropriate information, instruction, training and supervision to ensure that you can do your work safely and minimise the risk to your health. Your training should: Show you how to carry out your job safely; Include a competency assessment through demonstration before starting the work or starting each new task; A demonstration on how to use the necessary equipment and how to safely wear/use any protective gear, such as gloves, safety footwear and goggles; Explanation of health and safety policies and procedures; Workplace tour and understanding of the workplace layout; Introduction to your immediate supervisor, health and safety representative and workmates. At the start of your job your Supervisor should ensure that you are closely and competently supervised. Responsible, mature and necessary supervision must be provided by your Supervisor on an ongoing basis. It is critical that you understand your right to raise safety, descrimination, or harassment issues with your employer and to do so without fear of victimisation. You are also entitled, and encouraged to have someone represent you on workplace health and safety matters – a health and safety representative (HSR). If your workplace does not have an HSR, you or any other employee can request to set up a designated work group (DWG) structure. Once a DWG is established an HSR needs to be elected. If you are injured or involved in a ‘near miss’ safety incident you should immediately notify your employer. A near miss is an unplanned event that does not cause injury, damage or ill health but could do so and reporting them is a really important way of staying on top of safety. Reporting helps everyone to identify hazards and inappropriate conduct, prevent their occurrence and ensure your safety and equality.

topics.title: Common Workplace Hazards
topics.body: Whilst there are a number of people who are responsible for workplace safety you play a key role in identifying hazards and unsafe work practices. Some of the most common hazards in the workplace are: Work practices involving constant bending, lifting and twisting of your body Objects and liquids left on floors which result in slips, trips and falls Moving machinery parts which could crush or cut body parts Vehicles such as forklifts and trucks which may collide with workers Non-existent or confusing evacuation procedures Exposure to chemicals and other hazardous substances Bullying and harassment that results in psychological illness or physical assault Poor ergonomic design and practices that result in muscular strain

topics.title: Identifying Risks and Safety Issues
topics.body: Before commencing work, you should ensure that you know who to report safety issues to. Most workplaces will have procedures for handling issues when they arise; they’re often called issue resolution procedures. If there is no such procedure in your workplace you should notify your employer or Supervisor and they should follow it up for you. When issues are raised one or more of the following things should occur: 1. The issue raised will be assessed to determine the level of risk. 2. Individuals in the workplace who are responsible for health and safety will decide on the best solution. 3. A timeframe will be agreed for correcting the problem. 4. The effectiveness of the solution will be monitored.

topics.title: Action to take upon Identifying a Hazard
topics.body: The immediate action you should take upon identifying a hazard is: If you have not been given specific instructions on how to deal with any immediate hazards or incidents, you should ask the closest worker to isolate others from the immediate hazard whilst you notify your Supervisor. You should follow the instructions of your Supervisor or other appropriate persons unless this will expose you to risk. Complete an incident report form and give it to your Supervisor. Remember, you and your fellow workers have a responsibility to report all hazards to your employer, supervisor or workplace controller. If you are ever directed to re-commence work that you feel is unsafe, you should notify your employer immediately. If your employer isn’t treating your concerns seriously you have a right to notify an external body. You may also be required to participate in an ongoing process to prevent the re-occurrence of similar incidents or to determine the cause of the hazard.

topics.title: Hazardous Manual Task
topics.body: There are loads of hazards, which differ from one workplace to another, but there are some that are common to just about every workplace. Take a moment to think about some of the manual tasks that you may undertake on a daily basis. Some common manual tasks include: typing and keyboard entry filing using hand power tools handling live animals pushing or pulling objects such as trolleys, pallet jacks etc lifting and carrying objects such as boxes, materials, tools etc cleaning and general housekeeping activities maneuvering furniture and other objects handling/assisting patients/people As you are probably aware, many of the tasks we do on a daily basis involves manual operation, however just because it is manual does not mean it’s always hazardous!

topics.title: Responsibilities in the Workplace
topics.body: The Health and Safety Act and Regulations place duties on Officers, Person’s Conducting a Business or Undertaking (PCBUs)/Employers/Hosts and workers to manage the risk of musculoskeletal disorder associated with hazardous manual handling tasks. Each party is responsible for workplace safety, including manual tasks. In summary:

topics.title: What to do if you are injured
topics.body: Unfortunately injuries occur in even the safest of workplaces. It is essential that you understand what to do if you are injured at the workplace: Notify your Supervisor or First Aid Officer regardless of how minor the injury may appear at first. Keep your employer (HR) informed of your condition and progress at all times as they have a responsibility to report the incident. If you cannot attend work because of the injury or you incur related medical costs, hold discussions with your employer about the completion and lodgement of a workers compensation claim form. This should be done as soon as possible after the injury occurs.

topics.title: Emergency Management
topics.body: Fire, bomb threat, chemical exposure and personal assault can make you panic and act in a less than rational way and that’s why we practice getting evacuations and emergency management right. Know who your area warden is. That’s the person trained to tell you what to do and where to go in the event of an emergency. This person should be identified during your site and company specific induction prior to the commencement of work. Learn where the emergency stairs and evacuation points are for your building or floor. This may be shown on an emergency floor plan which should be displayed in your office. If you have an alarm system, know what each different alarm means. Find and memorise the location of fire extinguishers and manual alarms in your office. Learn where the emergency assembly points are, because this is where you need to go when you leave the building in an emergency and it’s critical that your area warden can account for you when you leave the building. Don’t use a lift unless your area warden says it’s safe to do so. Exit via the stairs where safe, and stay close to the handrail as this allows emergency officers to pass. If there’s smoke in the building remember to stay low and crawl to the emergency exit. If you’re confronted by an emergency try not to panic. I know it’s easy to say now, but panic doesn’t help anyone in an emergency. Follow the emergency management procedure if there’s one within your workplace. If there isn’t one provided in the site or company induction, follow it up with the responsible person.

topics.title: Stress
topics.body: Did you know workplace stress is the second most common cause of workplace compensation claims in Australia after manual handling? Stress claims cost businesses $10.11 billion p.a. due to loss of productivity and absenteeism. This figure is likely to be under-represented however as it doesn’t include unsuccessful claims and those who do not make a formal claim. So what does stress actually mean? The World Health Organisation defines stress as “the reaction people may have when presented with demands and pressures that are not matched to their knowledge and abilities and which challenge their ability to cope”. Stress can occur in a wide range of situations, is complex and typically has multiple causes. Many jobs involve negative factors that put unwanted pressure (stress) on the worker, leading to adverse consequences. Stress is not a disease or injury in itself, but can lead to mental and physical ill health, and can also be a factor in workplace incidents.

topics.title: What Causes Workplace Stress
topics.body:
Negative Stress

So, how is negative stress identified in the workplace? There are many different potential work-related stress hazards and risks in the workplace. You should be aware of systematic processes that the organisation undertakes to identify these hazards and risks. These processes should involve consultation with the workforce including you as a worker. Risks to psychological health in the workplace can largely be categorised as those relating to the social and physical work environment, the way that work is organised (system of work) and the way that work is managed. Some aspects of the social and physical environment that have the potential to cause harm are: role in the organisation career development, status and pay conflicting home/work demands physical work environment and equipment

topics.title: Stress and Systems of Work
topics.body: Issues relating to the way that work is organised (system of work) can include: the content and demands of the work the workload and pace of the work work schedules and working hours the extent of participation and control that people have over the work The way that work is managed can have harmful effects relating to: inadequate or unsupportive supervision lack of suitable information, instruction and training to enable employees to do their work

topics.title: Identifying & Managing Stress
topics.body: As a worker your employer owes you a duty of care. This duty of care extends to ensuring that your health and safety is not at risk; the meaning of health includes ‘psychological health’. Duty holders should be taking reasonable steps to eliminate or reduce the risk of negative stress. If you are a contractor, the on-hire/contracting firm can play a significant role in identifying and managing negative stress. Expect that your on-hire/contracting firm does the following: provides you with key job information (tasks, safety aspects, working hours including overtime, expected break times, remote work or working in isolation, reporting structure) maintains regular contact with you and offers opportunities to report any health and safety concerns associated with the contract assignment. For the Host, expect systems to manage the following areas: work environment systems of work work tasks If you feel you are exposed to negative stressors – report it to your supervisor/manager and (if appropriate) your onhire/contracting firm!

topics.body: You need to take some responsibility for identifying and managing stress, so here are some key points to consider:

topics.title: Sexual Harassment and the Law
topics.body: A single incident may amount to sexual harassment depending on the circumstances. For example, a single remark may be so offensive as to amount to sexual harassment in itself, but an unwanted invitation out may not constitute sexual harassment if it is not repeated. Sexual harassment is unlawful in any work-related context, including conferences, work functions, office parties and business or field trips and includes interactions with clients and customers. Sexual harassment is prohibited under Australian State and Federal legislation as well as international legislation.

topics.title: Workplace Harassment

topics.title: Victimisation
topics.body: It’s also against the law to threaten or treat people less favourably as a result of them raising or supporting allegations of discrimination, harassment or bullying. It may be considered victimisation if a person has suffered some form of detriment because they have, for example, lodged a complaint of discrimination or sexual harassment, attended a conciliation conference or reasonably asserted their rights, or supported someone else’s rights.

topics.title: How to Respond to Discrimination and Sexual Harassment
topics.body: If you believe you have been discriminated against, sexually or otherwise harassed or victimised in the workplace there are numerous options available to try and have the matter resolved. These include:

topics.title: Your Duty
topics.body: The health and safety of a co-worker doesn’t only relate to their physical wellbeing, it also includes their emotional or mental health. Treating someone in an undermining or unreasonable way negatively impacts upon their health and safety. You also have a duty to comply with any reasonable instruction provided to you and co-operate with any reasonable policies and procedures, such as a workplace bullying policy.

topics.title: What is not Bullying?
topics.body: Sometimes in the work environment decisions are made that you won’t like, or don’t agree with. There are also some situations where people in the workplace will have disagreements or differences of opinion and these are not generally considered to be workplace bullying. People can have differences and disagreements in the workplace without engaging in repeated, unreasonable behaviour that creates a risk to health and safety. The key point here is that just because you don’t agree with a decision or an opinion doesn’t mean that it amounts to bullying.
