modules.title: Construction Worker Safety
modules.description: This module focuses specifically on safety elements for general construction activities therefore it does not cover all aspects of construction or site-specific requirements and does not replace formal safety training. This module focuses on the following general risks and hazards:

topics.title: Learning Outcomes
topics.body: Once you’ve completed this module you should have a better understanding of the following the most common hazards and risks in general construction; what you can do to prevent these risks injuring someone or making them ill; and broad safe work principles that should be applied on a day to day basis. This module focuses specifically on safety elements for general construction activities, therefore it doesn’t cover all aspects of construction or site-specific requirements. The general safety topics that are covered within this module should be considered in conjunction with site specific induction and training.

topics.title: Manual handling
topics.body: Whilst your job will involve manual handling of some description it doesn’t have to be dangerous or hazardous. What is manual handling? Manual handling is using your own body’s strength to lift, lower, push, pull, carry, move, hold or restrain any object or person. Hazardous manual handling involves: repetitive or sustained application of force (e.g using a nail gun); repetitive work in awkward postures (e.g working on plasterboard ceiling); work with repetitive movements (e.g bricklaying); tasks that are difficult due to the degree of force applied (e.g lifting large bags of cement); exposure to sustained vibration (e.g using a jackhammer); and handling of unstable loads that are difficult to grasp or hold (e.g handling reo sheets or long lengths of timber) Types of manual handling injuries Manual handling can lead to injuries that mainly affect the bones and soft tissue structure. Examples include: sprains of ligaments; strains of muscles or tendons; injuries to the back, nerves, bones and joints; and soft tissue hernias. These injuries can occur suddenly from a single act of overexertion, for example: straining a back muscle whilst pushing a heavily laden trolley; and spraining a shoulder ligament whilst lifting a heavy object. It is more likely that an injury related to manual handling will develop over time from minor strains and gradual wear and tear.

topics.title: Working at heights (continued)
topics.body: The following situations would be considered hazardous on a construction site: working near unprotected open edges of floors or roofs; working near unguarded excavations, trenches, shafts or lift wells; and working on or near fragile/brittle surfaces such as skylights and fibreglass roofs It is a legal requirement that fall protection is provided to anyone who could fall more than 2 metres. The type of fall protection equipment must be selected using the following hierarchy: Firstly, eliminate the risk of falling. Ask yourself: can the work be completed on the ground or solid structure? For example prefabrication of roofs at ground level As it’s not always practical to eliminate working from a height the next control measure is to use passive fall prevention devices including: scaffolds (fixed or mobile) or perimeter guard railing If these two items aren’t practicable then work positioning systems must be used and these include: industrial rope access systems (they usually involve ropes, rope friction devices, harnesses and anchoring systems) travel restraint systems (these involve harnesses and anchoring systems used to limit the movement of the wearer or stop a fall) elevating work platform If the three risk control measures above are not practicable, fall injury prevention systems must be used. These systems don’t stop a fall but aim to minimise the distance someone can fall. These include: industrial safety nets catch platforms or a safety harness using fall arrest mechanisms If all of the four risk control measures above are not practicable then use a ladder or administrative system to control the risk of a fall. Ladders and administrative systems are poor ways to control the risk of a fall and must only be used if it can be demonstrated that other methods of fall protection are not reasonably practicable.

topics.title: Passive Fall Prevention - Scaffolds
topics.body: Scaffolds are a common means of providing a safe working platform for working at height. There is a wide variety of scaffolding systems available. Working platforms on scaffolds are generally rated as light, medium or heavy duty. The load limits provided below includes the weight of people (nominal weight of 80kg) plus the weight of any tools, materials or debris on the platform. Therefore, a light duty scaffold would be capable of supporting one worker and 145kg of tools and material. light duty – up to 225 kg per bay. This is suitable for plastering, painting, electrical work, and other light tasks; medium duty – up to 450 kg per bay. This is suitable for general trades work; heavy duty – up to 675 kg per bay. This is what is needed for bricklaying, concreting, demolition work and most other work tasks involving heavy loads or heavy impact forces; and special duty – has a designated allowable load as designed.

topics.title: Scaffolding (continued)
topics.body: Scaffolding should only be worked off if it: has been erected, altered or dismantled by a person who has received the relevant training. In the event that a person or object can fall more than 4 metres, the scaffold must be erected, altered or dismantled by or under the direct supervision of a licensed scaffolder. complies with the relevant Australian Standard; is on a stable and level foundation with proper base plates; properly braced and attached to the supporting structure; not overloaded; is fully planked and fitted with appropriate guardrails, mid-rail and toe boards on the working deck where a person or material could fall more than 2 metres; and has been fitted with a safe and secure temporary stairway or ladder to enable access to the working deck

topics.title: Mobile Scaffolds
topics.body: Where work is performed using mobile scaffolds, you should be aware of the following: when using on a soft surface such as soil, use steel channels or similar to provide a hard, flat surface; keep scaffolding well clear from powerlines, open floor edges and penetrations; never use mobile scaffolding unless the castors are locked to prevent movement; never move scaffolding whilst someone is on the scaffolding; and never access from the outside of the scaffold – use internal ladders only

topics.title: Suspended Scaffolds
topics.body: Suspended scaffolds include the following: swing stages; double-rope scaffolds; work cages; boatswain’s chairs; and false cars used in the construction of lifts Where work is performed using suspended scaffolds, you should be aware of the following: procedures and safe systems of work that have been implemented by the employer or principal contractor; you must be provided with specific information, training and instruction prior to commencing work; procedures that are in place for the rapid retrieval of suspended personnel in the event of an emergency; forms and channels of communication to be used between the cradle/chair and other workers to alert others on site in the event of an emergency; controls in place to prevent debris from falling onto workers in the cradle; where access and egress is not from the ground or a protected landing, safety harnesses must be used when accessing the cradle; and the cradle platform should be in a tidy condition with unobstructed access

topics.title: Elevating Work Platforms (EWP)
topics.body: Elevating Work Platforms: must not be used unless the operator has been trained in its use and safety rules; people operating EWPs with boom lengths exceeding 11 metres should have an appropriate certificate of competency; an anchored safety harness must always be worn whilst in a boom type EWP; and should only be used on a solid, level surface; the surface area should be checked to make sure that there are no penetrations or obstructions that could cause uncontrolled movement or overturning of the platform

topics.title: Perimeter guard railing
topics.body: Perimeter guard railing may be used to provide effective fall protection in the following areas: perimeters of buildings and other structures perimeters of skylights and other fragile roof material the edges of: roofs scaffolding work platforms walkways, Stairways and Landings shafts, Pits and other excavations openings in floor and roof structures A guardrail system must be relevant to the potential load and should: be installed by a competent person be 900-1100mm above the working surface incorporate a mid-rail/mesh panel and toe board be able to resist live loads that may be put on it not be used as the sole means of protection when the roof pitch is greater than 40 degrees. It should be used in conjunction with individual fall arrest systems and roof ladders. For example, the momentum of a person falling from a pitched roof will increase as the pitch (angle) of the roof increases. Therefore, an effective means of overcoming the fall hazard caused by a pitched roof is to place a scaffold deck at the perimeter edge.

topics.title: Work positioning systems - Fall arrest systems/Travel restraint systems
topics.body: As this is essentially Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) it should not be used unless other forms of fall protection have been considered and are deemed impractical. Work positioning systems require a higher level of competency and supervision than control measures which are higher in the hierarchy of control. Fall arrest systems: are an assembly of inter-connected components, comprising a harness connected to an anchorage, either directly or by means of a lanyard; should only be used where it’s not reasonably practicable to use a fall prevention measure; requires considerable skill to use safely, and in the event of an arrested fall, it is likely to cause some physical injury to the user; are intended to safely stop a worker falling an uncontrolled distance and reduce the impact of the fall; can be used where workers are required to carry out their work near an unprotected edge; and require a fall rescue plan to be developed and workers should not work alone.

topics.title: First Aid response
topics.body: First aid is the immediate treatment or care given to someone suffering from an injury or illness. If an incident occurs that results in injury, first aid can help reduce the severity of the injury and, in extreme cases, a quick response could mean the difference between life and death. The aims of first aid are to: preserve life; prevent illness or injury from becoming worse; relieve pain if possible; promote recovery; and protect the unconscious Employers and principal contractors have a legal responsibility to provide first aid facilities and the facilities must be appropriate to the hazards at the site. You will be provided with specific first aid details about your site first aid facilities during your site-specific induction. This induction should include: the nature of first aid facilities at the site; the location of first aid kits; and the names and work locations of person/s responsible for rendering first aid;

topics.title: Mobile Plant and traffic
topics.body: Mobile plant In your day to day activities, you will be exposed to a variety of mobile equipment such as forklifts, cranes, elevated work platforms and earth moving machinery. Mobile plant is very common on construction sites and a very high risk. In the construction industry there are 2 distinct areas that are required to be managed: 1. Managing mobile plant hazards in relation to the public. This includes: safe management of vehicles, mobile plant and equipment entering/exiting the site; and safe operation of mobile plant on footpaths or roads on the external boundaries of the construction site 2. Managing mobile plant operating within construction sites and ensuring the safe separation between pedestrians and mobile plant

topics.title: Managing mobile plant hazards in relation to the public
topics.body: It is a legal requirement for a Traffic Management Plan to be developed where construction activities have the potential to adversely affect external traffic and pedestrians. The following scenarios are some examples of situations that would trigger the requirement for a Traffic Management Plan: entry/exit from the construction site would dangerously impede or disrupt the flow of traffic on a highway or busy road; heavy vehicles or heavy mobile equipment is required to reverse out of the construction site; and closure of footpaths or roadway lanes for the purposes of construction equipment such as cranes and mobile equipment In the event that a Traffic Management Plan is required, it would need to include but is not limited to the following: develop a detailed risk assessment that addresses whether the company has sufficient resources to manage the traffic issue or whether it requires external professional assistance; obtain all necessary council permits for footpath and road closures; installation of advance warning signage to alert of truck entry/exit movements; and provision of traffic controllers with Stop/Go signage

topics.title: Managing mobile plant operating within construction sites
topics.body: The following items must be observed when dealing with the interaction of mobile equipment and pedestrians on a construction site: minimise the number of vehicles requiring access to the site; pedestrians must keep a safe distance from forklifts. Even at low speeds, an unexpected movement of the forklift can crush a bystander against a fixed structure or another vehicle; clear access routes through the site and one-way traffic where practicable; when a forklift is travelling around a corner or down a slope, when it accelerates or brakes, forces are developed that can result in it rolling sideways, tipping forwards or backwards. When a forklift overturns, the safest place for the operator is in the cabin with a seatbelt on. Almost every time an operator jumps from their forklift while it is overturning they are killed; and where practicable, separate Elevating Work Platforms from pedestrians through provision of barricading or flagging.

topics.title: On-site emergency response and evacuation procedures
topics.body: Emergencies can occur at any time, in any type of workplace. The aim is to eliminate or reduce the risk of injury or harm that may occur during an evacuation by undertaking a three-step process of: identifying potentially hazardous situations; assessing the risks; and implementing control measures. All workplaces must have evacuation procedures that have been specifically developed for the particular workplace or site and its specific hazards, and cover a range of potential incidents. The procedure must cover the safe, controlled and timely movement of people from the workplace/site in the event of: fire; explosion; bomb threat; collapse of the building or structural damage; and gas and chemical leaks It should also include the following: alarm signal for evacuation; how to exit the building safely; safe assembly point; and what to do and not do in the event of an emergency During your course of work you may be required to participate in an emergency evacuation drill as this is how the workplace/site tests to ensure the procedure is effective.

topics.title: Personal Protective Equipment
topics.body: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is the lowest in order of control priorities. These controls should not be relied on as the primary means of risk control until the options higher in the list of control priorities have been exhausted. PPE may be used in conjunction with other controls where the risk of exposure is high. The selection of appropriate PPE requires consideration of the hazards and risks of the work processes. The PPE may be required for a specific risk or to control multiple risks posed by the same hazard. For construction sites, the main types of PPE include the following: hard hats – to be worn at all times; safety footwear – to be worn at all times; hearing protection – to be worn in designated areas or when completing tasks with a high noise level (eg jackhammer); eye protection: must be worn in designated areas and when using power or machine tools; and face shields must be worn when working with acids and chemicals If welding is a common task the following must also be adhered to: welding goggles must be worn for gas welding and cutting; a welding helmet must be worn for electric arc welding; and in order to safely protect other persons, screens must be used to protect them from welding flashes

topics.title: Respiratory protection
topics.body: Respirators or face masks with an appropriate filter must be worn if you are exposed to hazardous chemical vapours, dust, fumes or fibres. Material Safety Data Sheets will enable you to determine whether respiratory protection is required for the task. Employers or principal contractors are required to provide the appropriate respiratory protection to their employees or contractors and provide training in how to use the PPE.

topics.title: Skin Protection and Sun (UV)
topics.body: Sunburn can occur to an unprotected person in as little as 15 minute’s exposure on a bright summer day. All types of sunburn can cause permanent or irreversible skin damage which can be the foundation for skin cancer later in life. You may not realise but the workplace is a major source of exposure to UV for many people. A major group of workers that are exposed to high levels of UV radiation are outdoor workers. Some health risks that are caused by over-exposure to UV radiation include the following: sunburn – ranging from redness to blistering; cataract of the eye lenses – ranges from decreased vision to blindness; skin carcinoma – malignant skin tumours; and malignant melanoma – severe cancer that can develop after excessive exposure to UV radiation As with other hazards in the workplace, worker exposure to UV radiation must be assessed and minimised by considering the following: attempt to re-organise outdoor work to avoid the UV peak of the day (when the UV index is above 3); utilised shaded areas (natural or artificial); wear PPE (clothing & sunglasses); and use SPF30+ sunscreen to unprotected skin

topics.title: Licenced, Ticketed and Certificated work
topics.body: A Certificate of Competency or equivalent High-Risk Work license is required for the operation of the following major and mobile equipment: tower cranes; portal boom cranes; scaffolding work; operating cranes, hoists and forklifts; removing specific types and amounts of asbestos; rigging work; and digging work

topics.title: License Validity
topics.body: You need to ensure that your license is valid and your Employer and Supervisor have a copy of your certification. Additionally, you are bound by the terms and conditions of the license that you hold. You must: comply with the terms and conditions of the license; advise the Authority of any changes to information that affects the license; keep evidence of the license for inspection by the Authority on request; apply for a replacement if the license is lost, stolen or destroyed; and ask the Authority to amend or cancel the license if necessary The Authority can suspend a license if the activities relating to it are not being carried out safely and competently. Items of major mobile plant should never be operated unless the intended operator has been fully trained and is licensed and competent in its use.

topics.title: Electrical hazards
topics.body: Electricity is invisible - this in itself makes it dangerous. It has great potential to seriously injure and kill. A person can receive critical injuries as a result of even very short exposures to everyday 240-volt single phase alternating current supply. Therefore, when working with electricity, it is important that the necessary precautions are taken. Regular and accurate maintenance of electrical outlets and supply plays a major part in minimising the chance of electrical accidents.

topics.title: Residual Current Devices (RCD)
topics.body: The power supply to all electrical equipment on construction sites must be protected by a Residual Current Devices (RCD). They should be tested regularly and all RCDs must be tested by a licensed electrician for tripping current There may be situations where temporary switchboards are required and they should have: a door, locking facility and RCDs; an insulated recess in the bottom for connecting extension leads; protection from the weather and mechanical damage; and A clearance of at least 1m in front of the board Some electrical hazards that may be present in the workplace or on-site include: frayed flexible supply cords; cracked electrical plant covers; flexible supply cords which have been run over by vehicles; electrical plant used in wet areas; and electrical plant which is moved frequently, such as concrete mixers.

topics.title: Residual Current Devices (RCD) (cont’d)
topics.body: These hazards can range from tree trimming near power lines to drilling a hole in a wall. Both these examples have the potential to injure or kill an employee if the hazards aren't appropriately controlled. Extension leads are used extensively on construction sites, however the following must be observed: they must be heavy duty; no extension lead should run from one floor to another on a multi-level site; leads should always be insulated to avoid contact with metal structures; and leads should be raised off the floor to protect them from water, damage and to provide clear access for personnel and vehicles A common cause of electrocution in the workplace/on-site or around sites is contact with overhead wires. This is because people can misjudge heights and distances between the ground and overhead wires when carrying equipment such as poles and ladders, or operating equipment with height extension, such as cranes.

topics.title: Power tools
topics.body: When working with power tools you need to be aware that: all portable electrical equipment, including power tools must be tested and tagged in accordance with the Australian Standard and by a licensed electrician; new purchased equipment must be tested and tagged prior to use to avoid poor manufacturing quality; RCDs should be tested monthly; the tagging system should follow the colours listed in the Australian Standard to avoid confusion

topics.title: Permit Work (Confined spaces, Hot and cold work)
topics.body: Some activities in the construction industry are inherently hazardous to workers safety and health such as: Hot Work Hot work is a term used to describe heat-producing operations such as welding, flame cutting and grinding. Hot work presents two significant hazards; open flames or flying sparks that can ignite flammable gases and vapours production of toxic fumes and gases. Confined Spaces Means an enclosed or partially enclosed space that: is not intended or designed primarily as a place of work; is at atmospheric pressure while persons are in it; may have an atmosphere with potentially harmful contaminants, an unsafe level of oxygen or stored substances that may cause engulfment; and may (but need not) have restricted means of entry and exit. Examples of confined spaces include air conditioning ducts, crawl spaces, pits, trenches, pipes, sewers or box beams.

topics.title: Confined Space (continued)
topics.body: When you are working in confined spaces, it is a legal requirement: to ensure that all hazards associated with a confined space are identified and this must be completed in conjunction with a Health and Safety Representative; to be inducted into the relevant work procedures for the confined space and receive full instruction, information and training in relation to the hazards and risks posed by the confined space; and that a sign is erected in the immediate vicinity of the confined space identifying the confined space and notifying that entry can only be gained after receiving a confined space entry permit.

topics.title: Confined Space Entry Permit
topics.body: Confined Space Entry Permit requirements are outlined below: applies to only one confined space and must provide details of the area; must name the employees permitted to enter the confined space and measures to be taken to control the risks; requires continuous communication between the person appointed for watch outside the confined space, and the person working inside the space; requires procedures to be in place to know when there is a person in a confined space and when they have exited; have in place emergency procedures that cover: rescue first Aid PPE Ensure that prior to working in a confined space: plant or services that are connected must be isolated or de-energised; safe oxygen levels are established; the space is purged of any contaminant; if it’s not reasonably practicable for all contaminants to be removed to below the acceptable levels, then air-supply respiratory protective equipment must be supplied; and if there is a likelihood of fire or explosion, then an ignition source must not be introduced in to the confined space

topics.title: Working with Asbestos
topics.body: The dangers associated with asbestos are widely known to contribute to lung cancer, asbestosis and mesothelioma, therefore you need to be aware of the following when working with asbestos: before demolition or refurbishment work occurs, all areas that may contain asbestos must be identified; if asbestos is found or suspected in the workplace or on-site, it must not be disturbed and the Supervisor must be notified immediately; licensing for the removal of asbestos is to ensure that only workers who possess the required knowledge, skills and safe systems of work to do the job safely will be able to perform the work; it is a requirement that business operators removing more than ten square metres of bonded asbestos, including asbestos cement material, in a workplace will need to have completed an approved training course and hold an asbestos license; a permit to work system is implemented as it provides a systematic disciplined approach to assessing the risks of a job and specifying the precautions to be taken when performing work in a hazardous environment.

topics.title: Asbestos Permit to Work System
topics.body: The asbestos permit to work system: specifies the work to be done and the equipment to be used; specifies the precautions to be taken when performing the task; gives permission for work to start; advises personnel within the workplace that work is being performed; provides a check to ensure that all safety considerations have been taken into account, including the validity of permits and certificates and compliance to policies and procedures; and on completion of work it provides a checking mechanism that all work has been completed.

topics.title: Stress
topics.body: Did you know workplace stress is the second most common cause of workplace compensation claims in Australia after manual handling? Stress claims cost businesses $10.11 billion p.a. due to loss of productivity and absenteeism. This figure is likely to be under-represented however as it doesn’t include unsuccessful claims and those who do not make a formal claim. So what does stress actually mean? The World Health Organisation defines stress as “the reaction people may have when presented with demands and pressures that are not matched to their knowledge and abilities and which challenge their ability to cope”. Stress can occur in a wide range of situations, is complex and typically has multiple causes. Many jobs involve negative factors that put unwanted pressure (stress) on the worker, leading to adverse consequences. Stress is not a disease or injury in itself, but can lead to mental and physical ill health, and can also be a factor in workplace incidents.

topics.title: Negative Stress
topics.body: So, how is negative stress identified in the workplace? There are many different potential work-related stress hazards and risks in the workplace. You should be aware of systematic processes that the organisation undertakes to identify these hazards and risks. These processes should involve consultation with the workforce including you as a worker. Risks to psychological health in the workplace can largely be categorised as those relating to the social and physical work environment, the way that work is organised (system of work) and the way that work is managed. Some aspects of the social and physical environment that have the potential to cause harm are: role in the organisation career development, status and pay conflicting home/work demands physical work environment and equipment

topics.title: Stress and Systems of Work
topics.body: Issues relating to the way that work is organised (system of work) can include: the content and demands of the work the workload and pace of the work work schedules and working hours the extent of participation and control that people have over the work The way that work is managed can have harmful effects relating to: inadequate or unsupportive supervision lack of suitable information, instruction and training to enable employees to do their work

topics.title: Identifying & Managing Stress
topics.body: As a worker your employer owes you a duty of care. This duty of care extends to ensuring that your health and safety is not at risk; the meaning of health includes ‘psychological health’. Duty holders should be taking reasonable steps to eliminate or reduce the risk of negative stress. If you are a contractor, the on-hire/contracting firm can play a significant role in identifying and managing negative stress. Expect that your on-hire/contracting firm does the following: provides you with key job information (tasks, safety aspects, working hours including overtime, expected break times, remote work or working in isolation, reporting structure) maintains regular contact with you and offers opportunities to report any health and safety concerns associated with the contract assignment. For the Host, expect systems to manage the following areas: work environment systems of work work tasks If you feel you are exposed to negative stressors – report it to your supervisor/manager and (if appropriate) your onhire/contracting firm!

topics.title: Tips for dealing with Workplace Stress
topics.body:
You need to take some responsibility for identifying and managing stress, so here are some key points to consider:

Summary

In finishing up I want to remind you that it’s critical that you take a proactive approach to safety when working on a construction site. Any time you identify a hazard, it is important that you report it to your Supervisor, Foreman or OHS Rep, as this is one of the most important ways that health and safety is improved in the workplace. This training has provided you with the most common hazards and risks in construction work, what you can do to prevent these risks injuring someone and some broad safe work principles. It is important that you familiarise yourself with the high risk hazards and tasks in your workplace prior to commencing work. Remember the following essentials: report hazards as soon as you identify them, this is the best way to minimize injury; eliminating the hazard is the best way to reduce the risk; administrative and PPE controls are the lowest way of controlling risk; keeping fit can help reduce the risk of manual handling related injuries; and mobile equipment and pedestrians don’t mix

Slips, trips and falls
